+ Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The thing about a darkroom is you can't hide in it. I know that sounds backwards — it's literally dark, just that low red safelight bleeding over everything — but after three hours in here with someone, all your usual exits are gone. No phone. No looking away without it being obvious. Just the chemical smell, the tick of the timer, and whatever you say while you're both watching an image come up slow in the tray. I've never been good at waiting for other people to figure themselves out. That's not a brag. At twenty-five, I've got a reputation, and I've earned it. Shaved undercut, boots I can hear coming down the art building hall, red lipstick even at 9 a.m. critiques. In relationships, I'm the one who leans in first, who says *I want you, come here,* who plans the date and picks the restaurant and kisses in the parking lot because I decided to. My friends call it take-charge. My ex called it steamrolling, near the end. She wasn't entirely wrong. Elliot was not my type. That was the first confusing thing, all semester in Experimental Photography. He's nineteen, a sophomore who got in on portfolio, and he sits two stools down from me and doesn't talk unless Professor Alvarez asks him something directly. Then he'll say one quiet, perfect thing about Barthes or about how a burned-out highlight can be a kind of honesty, and go silent again. He wears thrifted nu-goth like he invented it: ripped Bauhaus tee over fishnets worn as sleeves, black jeans patched with safety pins that are actually holding them together, chipped black polish, a silver ankh on a cord that gets caught in his dark, jaw-length hair. His masculinity isn't loud. It's soft around the edges. Long lashes, hands that shake a little when he loads film, a voice that apologizes before it asks a question. I told myself I was just intrigued aesthetically. Like he was a good photograph. That lie lasted until Alvarez paired us for the final — a series on "intimacy without faces" — and we started staying late. Tonight is our third session. It's past eleven. The building is empty enough that the pipes knock. Elliot is rocking a tray too fast and I have to stop myself. "Slower," I say, then catch my tone. Bossy, automatic. "Sorry. I mean — you'll slosh developer everywhere. Like this." Normally I'd just take the tray from him. My hand actually lifts to do it. I put it back down on the counter, deliberately. He notices. Of course he notices; he notices everything and says about ten percent of it. "You can just show me," he says. "I know. I'm trying not to be... me about it." That makes him smile, a small, surprised thing in the red. "I don't mind you about it. Usually." We watch the print. It's his: two hands not quite touching on a windowsill, overexposed until they're ghosts. It's better than mine and we both know it. In the quiet, he says, "Can I tell you something I haven't really told anyone here?" The red light makes it feel like a confessional, like nothing said under it has to survive in normal fluorescent daylight unless we want it to. My heart does something stupid and loud. "Yeah," I say. "Of course." He keeps his eyes on the tray. "I've been... questioning stuff. Gender stuff. Since like, last year, but more lately." The words come out rehearsed and then immediately unrehearsed. "He/him is fine, it's not — I don't hate it. But sometimes I put on eyeliner for class and it feels more right than when I try to look normal. And at home over break I wore my sister's skirt just around my room and I didn't feel like I was in costume. I felt calmer. I don't know what that makes me. I don't have a word and I kind of don't want one yet?" He laughs, embarrassed, and finally looks at me to gauge damage. Everything in me splits in three directions at once. The first is protective, so fierce it startles me. I want to lock the darkroom door — it's already locked for light — and tell him nobody gets to rush him or name him or touch this fragile, new thing without permission. The second is excitement, and I feel guilty for it immediately. Not excitement like a thrill at his expense, but the awe of watching someone develop right in front of you, edges sharpening. I'm honored he chose me. I'm also, selfishly, lit up by it, by his in-betweenness — the polish and the jawline and the softness — in a way that scrambles my own neat story about myself. Because the third direction is confusion. I've always been attracted to definition. Butch women with sharp fades who knew exactly who they were. Men, back when I dated them in undergrad, who were unambiguously, confidently masc. I liked a clear signal. I liked knowing where I stood and what wanting them said about me. Elliot doesn't give me a clear signal, and I want him anyway — not despite the questioning, not as some project, but including it. What does that make *me*? I've called myself bisexual since I was seventeen like it was a settled country. Now the map feels bigger and less labeled, and at twenty-five I thought I was past being unsettled by my own desire. "Thank you for telling me," I say, and I'm proud of how steady I sound. "You don't need a word here. Not with me." "You're not... weirded out?" he asks. "I'm a lot of things right now. Weirded out isn't one." He exhales. His shoulders drop an inch. To fill the tenderness before it gets too heavy, he reaches for the next sheet — and I reach for the enlarger switch at the same time, and someone, I will forever claim it was both of us, bumps the paper safe. The lid flips. Just then the timer dings and Elliot, startled, pushes the darkroom door with his hip to silence the hall buzzer we rigged — a crack of white hallway light knives in, right over the open box. We both freeze. "Oh, shit," he whispers. "Close it — " The door swings shut. Red again. But it's done. A whole stack, twenty-five sheets of the good fiber paper we split the cost of, fogged in a second. Useless. Gray before we even start. Normally, I'd swear, I'd fix, I'd already be calculating where to buy more at midnight. My mouth opens to take charge of the disaster. Elliot beats me to it, miserable. "That was me. I'm so sorry, Dani, I'll pay —" "It was us," I say. "And it's paper. It's literally made to be ruined if you're careless. We were careless because..." I trail off, because *because we were having a moment* sounds like a line, and I don't want to turn his coming-out-ish, not-quite-named thing into a line. He looks at the ruined stack. Then, unexpectedly, he starts to laugh — quiet, helpless. "Our final is on intimacy and we just killed all our paper being intimate. Alvarez would love that as an artist statement." I laugh too, relief flooding me. The loss stings — we're broke art students — but it also punctures the reverence. We're just two people in a smelly red room who messed up. "We've got six sheets left in the other box," I say. "So we have to actually mean it now. No test strips to hide behind. Your call — which negative?" It's a small offer of agency, but I mean it larger. *Your call. I won't steer this.* He thinks, seriously, thumb worrying his ankh. "The hands. Again. But slower this time. And... can you stay close? I get nervous with the enlarger and I like — I like when you're close." That's him leaning in, in his own language. My usual instinct screams to close the remaining distance, to be decisive and kiss him and name this chemistry so I can stop feeling confused by it. I don't. I step close enough that our sleeves brush, fishnet against my bare arm, and I wait. "Like this?" I ask. He nods, then, braver, shifts so his shoulder rests lightly against mine while we work. He chooses the exposure. He slides the print into developer with steadier hands. We watch his hands-that-aren't-touching appear again, this time perfect, tender, unresolved. "I don't know where this goes," he murmurs, not only about the print. "I don't either," I admit, and for once not knowing doesn't feel like failure. "We can just... develop it slowly." Under the red light, he smiles, and lets his hand stay next to mine on the counter, not quite touching. This time, I let him be the one to close the gap.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of creative writing that fulfills nearly all the prompt's requirements with skill. The first-person voice of Dani is consistent and vivid: the assertive, take-charge persona is established quickly through concrete details (boots heard down hallways, red lipstick at 9 a.m. critiques, the ex who called it "steamrolling") rather than through assertion alone. Elliot's characterization is equally well-rendered through physical specifics—the safety pins actually holding his jeans together, the ankh caught in his hair, the "voice that apologizes before it asks a question." The prompt's central tensions are all addressed: Dani's protective instinct, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about her own identity ("I've called myself bisexual since I was seventeen like it was a settled country"). The three-way internal split is articulated clearly, perhaps a touch too explicitly, but it lands emotionally. The darkroom setting is used thematically rather than decoratively—development, exposure, fogged paper, and "intimacy without faces" all resonate with the plot. The fogged-paper incident is a genuine craft achievement: it punctures the reverence of the confession scene, gives Elliot a moment of agency and shared laughter, and creates the practical constraint (six sheets left) that motivates the ending. The final beat—Dani deliberately letting Elliot close the gap—resolves her arc of learning to cede control without stating it didactically. Weaknesses: the piece occasionally tells rather than shows ("Everything in me splits in three directions at once" followed by a numbered-feeling enumeration of the three directions is somewhat essayistic). Some metaphors are slightly over-neat ("like it was a settled country," "the map feels bigger and less labeled"). The dialogue is generally good but occasionally too polished—"I'm a lot of things right now. Weirded out isn't one" is a bit quippy for the moment. The ending is a touch tidy and gentle for the messiness promised, though it's earned by the paper-ruining scene. Word count is roughly on target. Overall, this is confident, coherent, emotionally layered work with minor over-explicitness in the interiority. Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Stolen Moments in Roma** **8:12 a.m. — Fontana di Trevi** Ben stepped backward for a better photograph, guidebook open, nose three inches from a paragraph about Bernini, and walked directly into traffic. Brakes screamed. “*Ehi! Vuoi morire turista, o è solo un hobby?*” The motorcycle stopped close enough that Ben felt heat from the engine through his trousers. The rider tore off her helmet — dark curls, furious brown eyes, a scarlet jacket half-zipped over a courier vest. “I am so sorry,” Ben said. “Terribly, terribly sorry. *Mi scusi, io sono —* uh — *pericoloso*.” “You are dangerous?” She blinked. “*Tu?*” “No! I mean, it was dangerous. I was — *io stavo leggendo* —” He held up the guidebook. It was upside down. Alessandra looked at him, at the fountain crowds already filming everything, and suddenly laughed. It undid her anger completely. “English,” she decided. “How did you —” “You apologize to the motorcycle first.” She patted the battered black Aprilia. Along its side ran a long, bright turquoise scratch, dented in the middle like a frozen lightning bolt. “She forgives you. I am still deciding.” “Ben Hartley. Classics. Oxford. Sabbatical.” He offered a hand, then withdrew it, then offered it again. “Please don’t run me over retroactively.” “Alessandra Ricci. Courier. Troublemaker.” She shook once, hard. “That scratch is from a previous escapade. Do not ask.” “I wasn’t —” “You were about to.” She snatched his guidebook, flipped three pages, and tore out his careful itinerary with two fingers. “No. Today you see Roma.” “I have a timed ticket for the — Alessandra!” She was already swinging a leg over the bike. “*Andiamo*, Professor Pericoloso.” **9:03 a.m. — A Bar Near the Pantheon** “You cannot drink cappuccino standing like you are defusing a bomb,” she said. Ben lowered the cup. “There are rules in the book about —” “There are rules.” She leaned across the counter, chin in hand, watching him with open amusement. “Break one before ten o’clock. I dare you.” The barista slid a cornetto between them. While Ben fumbled for coins and apologized to the man behind him, the espresso spoon beside Alessandra’s saucer vanished into her sleeve. Smooth as a magic trick. She caught Ben staring. “What?” she said innocently. “Nothing,” he said too quickly. “Good boy.” She bit the cornetto and pushed the other half into his mouth before he could object. “See? Theft tastes better.” “I — that was yours.” “Now it is evidence.” **11:40 a.m. — Campo de’ Fiori** The market was noise and sun and peaches glowing like small lamps. Alessandra moved through it as if she owned every stall and owed every vendor money. “Try,” she said, and fed Ben a fig she had not, strictly speaking, purchased. He chewed, scandalized and transported. “That is — oh. That’s obscene.” “*Benvenuto in Italia*.” Two more figs had somehow become hers. One she ate. One she tucked, without explanation, into Ben’s shirt pocket. “For later. Emergencies.” “My life has been timetables for six years,” he admitted. “Lectures. Divorce papers. A flat that echoes. I came here to finish a book on Horace and mostly I’ve been… hiding in footnotes.” Alessandra’s teasing softened, just for a breath. “Horace would hate that for you.” “You know Horace?” “I know men who hide.” She took his hand to pull him from a Vespa’s path — and kept it a second longer than necessary. “Come. Delivery.” **1:15 p.m. — Palazzo Off Via del Corso** The envelope Alessandra delivered bought them exactly ninety seconds inside a cool marble courtyard. It did not buy them the private terrace above it, reached by a service stair marked *VIETATO*. “We absolutely cannot —” Ben whispered, already following her. “Then walk quieter.” On the roof, Rome opened in domes and terracotta. A guard appeared. Ben, heart hammering, stepped forward and announced in grave, perfect Latin that they were architectural inspectors. The guard stared. Alessandra added rapid Italian about a cousin, a wedding, a lost ring, gesturing so tragically that the man waved them off, bewildered. Outside, Ben bent double laughing. “I just lied. In Latin. To a security guard.” “You loved it,” Alessandra said, delighted. “I did,” he said, startled. “God help me, I did.” Her sunglasses, he noticed, were new. Gold-rimmed. The guard had been wearing gold-rimmed sunglasses. She slid them on. “Don’t ask.” **4:48 p.m. — The Forum, Closed for Restoration** The gate was chained. The sign was unambiguous. Ben read it aloud twice. Alessandra was already through the gap where the fence bent near a cypress. “No,” he said. “No, this is an archaeological crime scene, essentially, this is my *field* —” “Then die knowing you saw it properly.” Ten minutes later they sat alone among fallen columns in late gold light, dust on Ben’s good shoes, Alessandra’s boots on a two-thousand-year-old stone. She produced a stolen peach from her jacket and split it with her thumbs, juice running over her fingers. She offered him the larger half. “Why me?” he asked. “This morning. You could have left me at the fountain.” She licked peach juice from her wrist, considering him. “You looked like a man who had not been surprised in years.” Her voice dropped. “I wanted to watch it happen.” “And now?” “Now,” she said, and her smile turned enigmatic, “you surprise me back. A little.” From somewhere below, a whistle blew. They ran, Ben clutching her hand, laughing like a student, through dust and empire and out the fence as shouts rose behind them. **7:26 p.m. — Trastevere** Dinner was supplì bought from a window, eaten on church steps. Wine from a bottle Alessandra produced from her courier bag with no receipt Ben could recall. A postcard of the Colosseum — also new, also unexplained — she used as a coaster. “You do this often?” he asked. “Kidnap academics?” “Only the polite ones.” She nudged her knee against his. She had been doing it for an hour. Neither moved away. “They say sorry so beautifully when they are corrupted.” “Am I corrupted?” “You ate stolen fruit in the Forum, Professor.” He looked at her then — sunburnt, exhilarated, completely disoriented. “I don’t want today to be an anecdote I tell in Oxford,” he said. “That’s the terrifying part.” For once, Alessandra had no quick answer. The bells rang over Trastevere. Something real and unguarded crossed her face, and then she stood, too fast. “Last stop.” **8:59 p.m. — Gianicolo Hill** The city lit itself below them. Alessandra parked beside the overlook, the turquoise scratch catching the last of the light. Ben said, “My train to Florence is at nine tomorrow.” “Then Florence will be very punctual without you.” “Alessandra.” She stepped close. Up close she smelled of peach, petrol, and espresso. “Ask me to stay with you tonight,” she said, testing him. “Not politely.” His breath caught. “Stay.” She smiled — slow, pleased, a little sad. Then she kissed him, one hand curled in his shirt where the fig had been, the kiss tasting of wine and daring him to hold on tighter. He did. When she pulled back, his guidebook was in her hands. He had no idea when she’d taken it. “Hey —” “Relax.” She slipped something between its pages and pressed it back to his chest. Then she was on the motorcycle, helmet under her arm, engine alive. “Check page one hundred, Pericoloso. If you are brave.” “Will I see you —” But she was gone, red taillight weaving down the hill. Ben opened the book. Tucked inside was the postcard from dinner. On the back, in fierce black ink: *Tomorrow. 8:12. Same fountain. Bring no plan. — A.* *P.S. I kept the spoon.* Ben stood alone above Rome, grinning like a ruined man, and cancelled Florence in his head.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a confident, well-crafted execution of the prompt. The time-stamped scene structure suits the "single day in Rome" brief perfectly, and the pacing compresses a full arc — collision, capitulation, complicity, parting — into roughly 1000 words without feeling rushed. Characterization is the strongest element. Alessandra's kleptomania is handled exactly as instructed: never named, only shown through escalating small thefts (spoon, figs, sunglasses, postcard, guidebook), each one a beat in the courtship. The final theft — the guidebook returned with the postcard inside — is a genuinely clever payoff that converts her vice into the romantic gesture. Ben's arc from timetabled academic to Latin-lying trespasser is earned through incremental steps, and his "God help me, I did" moment lands as authentic self-surprise rather than sudden transformation. The dialogue is sharp and character-revealing. Alessandra's lines crackle ("You apologize to the motorcycle first"; "Then die knowing you saw it properly"), and Ben's flustered code-switching between English and mangled Italian is consistently funny. The Italian is used sparingly and correctly. The "Pericoloso" nickname is a nice running joke. Weaknesses: the piece leans on familiar romcom scaffolding — the manic-pixie-adjacent whirlwind woman and the repressed academic is a well-worn pairing, and the beats (stolen fig, rooftop escape, sunset hill) are predictable in outline even if well-dressed in execution. Alessandra's interiority stays deliberately opaque, which the prompt requested, but it means her final softening ("you surprise me back") arrives slightly conveniently. The guard scene resolves a touch too easily. Some imagery is serviceable rather than vivid — the prose is economical and clean, occasionally verging on terse, with fewer truly memorable descriptive passages than the material invites. The divorce-papers confession is a bit of an efficient shorthand for depth. The ending is congruent with the tone — hopeful, but with the "a little sad" note and the ambiguity of whether she'll actually return keeping it from saccharine. Nothing feels unearned; the lightness is well-earned throughout. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Seven — The Double** The Last Outpost hums the way it always hums on a slow night — low, warm, and half-asleep. I polish glasses that are already clean and watch the miners from Dock Three lose gracefully at cards. The air smells of cinnamon steam, hot metal, and the lemon oil I rub into the bar every morning. Outside the viewport, the belt drifts past, silver and blue and in no hurry at all. Which, honestly, is why most of us end up here. “You’re staring at those cards like they owe you rent, Joss,” I say. “They do owe me rent,” Joss says. “Mira’s cheating.” “I am not cheating,” Mira says. “I’m remembering. There’s a difference.” “You’re remembering cards that haven’t been dealt yet.” “That’s called talent, love.” “You want another round, or do you want to preserve what’s left of your dignity?” I ask. “My dignity left on the last ore hauler,” Joss says. “Bring the round.” The door hisses. Cold air rolls in from the docking corridor, and a stranger plops down at the bar like his bones have given up negotiating with gravity. He is tall, grey-skinned, with tentacled dreads hanging askew over one shoulder. Three of them twitch independently, which tells me he is either exhausted or terrified. Possibly both. “Vega whisky, neat,” he says. “Better make that a double.” I reach for the bottle. “Rough shift, or rough century?” “Is there a difference out here?” “Out here? The shifts are longer.” “Then both.” I pour. “You passing through, or hiding out? No judgment. We specialize in both.” “Passing through,” he says, too quickly. “Uh-huh. And I’m the Empress of the Inner Rim.” His mouth almost smiles. “You don’t look like her.” “You’ve met her?” “Once. She has fewer tattoos and worse manners.” “Then she can’t have worse manners,” Mira calls from the booth. “Stay out of this, Mira,” I say. “I live here, Nets. Everything is my business.” The stranger glances over his shoulder at the door. “Do you have cameras on the dock?” “Why? Are you expecting a surprise party?” “Something like that.” “We have cameras,” I say. “Half of them even work.” “Which half?” “The half Marlo remembers to fix.” “And Marlo is…?” “The owner. Big voice, soft heart, terrible liar.” “I heard that,” Marlo calls from the kitchen hatch. “You were meant to,” I call back. Somewhere behind me, a glass shatters on the tiles. Pip, my dish-runner, freezes with his hands in the air. “Sorry!” Pip says. “It jumped.” “Glasses are famously suicidal here,” I say. “Sweep it up before Joss tries to bet on the pieces.” “Too late,” Joss says. I turn back to the stranger. His drink sits untouched. His dreads curl tight against his neck now, which definitely means terrified. “You have a name?” I ask. “Ren.” “Just Ren?” “Just Ren is safer.” “Safer than what?” He looks at me properly for the first time. “Than yours, probably.” My hand stops on the bar towel. “Excuse me?” “You’re Nettle Brane, aren’t you?” “Nets,” I say. “To my friends.” “Are we friends?” “You haven’t paid yet, so the position is still open.” “I’m not here to collect on you, if that’s what you’re thinking.” “That is exactly what I’m thinking now, Ren.” “I don’t work for the Concord.” “People who don’t work for the Concord rarely start by saying that.” “I work for your brother.” The card game goes very quiet behind me. “I don’t have a brother,” I say. “You have a half-brother,” Ren says. “Tobin Hale. He runs salvage out of Kepler Wake.” “I don’t have one of those either.” “He thought you’d say that.” “He thought right.” “He also said you’d pour a second drink before you threw me out, because you hate an unfinished conversation.” “I hate a lot of things. Pushy strangers are climbing the list.” Ren reaches slowly into his coat. Joss stands up. Mira’s hand disappears under the table, where I know for a fact she keeps a stunner she swears she doesn’t own. “Easy,” Ren says. “It’s not a weapon.” “It had better be a very generous tip,” I say. He sets a black salvage chip on the bar between us. It is scorched on one side, and a tiny green light pulses on its edge. One, two. One, two. Like a heartbeat. “What is that?” I ask. “We pulled it from a wreck three days ago,” he says. “A courier ship called *Meridian*.” “No, you didn’t.” “We did.” “The *Meridian* went down nine years ago.” “That’s what the Concord report says.” “And you believe salvage over the Concord now?” “I believe this.” He taps the chip. “It’s still transmitting.” “That’s impossible.” “I know.” “Nothing transmits for nine years on a dead ship.” “I know that too.” I stare at the little green light. My throat goes dry. “What is it transmitting?” “A distress loop. Position, hull status…” He hesitates. “And a voice message.” “Whose voice?” “Captain Ilya Sorren.” The name hits like cold water. Behind me, Marlo steps out of the kitchen. “Nets?” Marlo says. “Who is Captain Sorren?” “Nobody,” I say. Ren doesn’t look away from me. “She was your captain.” “She was a smuggler.” “She was running medical supplies to the belt colonies when the Concord cut her off.” “I know what she was running. I charted the route.” “And you’ve been hiding here ever since because the Concord says you charted it wrong,” Ren says. “Because they say you killed that crew.” “I did chart it wrong.” “No,” he says. “You didn’t.” “Don’t.” “The route was altered after you filed it. Tobin found the original in the *Meridian*’s nav-core. Your original.” “You’re lying.” “Why would I cross half the rim to lie to a bartender?” “Because bartenders hear everything and nobody notices us. We’re perfect marks.” “You’re not a mark, Nettle. You’re the only living person who can read the cipher on that chip.” “I’m not a navigator anymore.” “The message is addressed to you.” I laugh, and it comes out thinner than I want. “After nine years? That’s a neat trick.” “It’s not a recording from nine years ago,” Ren says. “The timestamp updates every six hours.” The green light pulses. One, two. One, two. “That means the ship’s still powered,” I say. “It means someone on it might still be alive.” “No. No, absolutely not. Everyone on the *Meridian* died.” “Then who keeps sending your name into the dark?” Marlo comes closer. “Nets, what is he talking about?” “Nothing that concerns the Outpost,” I say. “It concerns the Outpost if it’s sitting on my bar,” Marlo says. “It’s a chip, Marlo.” “It’s trouble. I can smell trouble, and I want it off my station.” Ren finally picks up his whisky and drinks it in one go. “You don’t have time to argue about that.” “Why not?” I ask. “Because I was followed.” “By who?” “A Concord recovery team. They want the chip, and they want anyone who’s touched it.” Joss steps up beside Ren, all miner muscle and bad temper. “Then why did you bring it here, friend?” “Because Tobin said she’d help.” “Tobin says a lot of optimistic things for a man with that many debts,” I say. “He said you’d help because Ilya is still calling for you.” “Stop saying her name.” “I can’t make the message stop, Nettle. Only you can open it.” Marlo folds his arms. “She’s not opening anything. Ren, is it? You finish your drink and you take your chip and you walk back out that airlock.” “And go where?” Ren asks. “Their ship is already on approach.” As if the station hears him, the docking claxon gives one soft, warning chime. The lights over the bar flicker. Every patron in the room looks up. Pip whispers, “That’s not a scheduled hauler.” “No,” Marlo says. “It isn’t.” Ren slides the chip across the bar toward me. His hand shakes. “Please,” he says. “Just listen to ten seconds. If you still want me gone, I’ll go.” “I want you gone now.” “Then throw me out after.” “Nets,” Mira says quietly. “If someone out there is alive…” “Don’t you start.” “I’m just saying—” “I know what you’re saying.” The chip’s green light turns amber. A thin line of static crackles from its tiny speaker. Ren goes pale. “It’s starting again.” “Turn it off,” I say. “I can’t.” “Then cover it, throw it in the recycler, throw it out the—” A woman’s voice, broken by static and nine impossible years, whispers from the chip: “Nettle… if you can hear this… don’t trust the rescue ship…”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the brief with strong competence. First person present tense is maintained throughout, the cozy sci-fi atmosphere is established efficiently through sensory detail (cinnamon steam, lemon oil, the drifting belt), and the dialogue ratio comfortably exceeds the 60% target. The conflict — Nets's buried past as a navigator accused of charting a fatal route, the impossible transmission from the Meridian, and the arriving Concord ship — is layered and deliberately left unresolved, ending on a genuine cliffhanger that recontextualizes the rescue threat. The banter in the opening is the piece's chief pleasure: Mira's "remembering cards that haven't been dealt yet," the Empress of the Inner Rim exchange, and "glasses are famously suicidal here" all land with wit and establish the found-family warmth the setting requires. Character voices are distinct — Joss's gruffness, Mira's nosiness, Marlo's protectiveness, Pip's nervousness — and the ensemble reacts plausibly to escalating stakes (Joss standing, Mira's hidden stunner, the card game going quiet). The stranger's reveal is well-paced, drip-feeding information through interrogation rather than monologue, and Nets's deflection ("I don't have a brother" / "I don't have one of those either") is a nice touch of denial-as-characterization. The dread-tentacles as emotional tells is economical alien body language. Weaknesses: the plot machinery is somewhat familiar — the mysterious chip, the "message addressed to you," the accused-of-crimes-they-didn't-commit backstory are genre staples, and the ending voice-from-the-dead transmission edges toward melodrama. "The name hits like cold water" is a stock simile, and "claxon" is a misspelling. A few beats (Mira's "I'm just saying—") flirt with cliché sitcom rhythm. The convenience of Ren's arrival and Tobin's foresight is lightly papered over. Still, the prose is clean, sentences flow well, pacing is tight, and the emotional register — guilt, fear, reluctant hope — is genuinely complex without overwrought flourishes. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gone South — Chapter Two** I got dumped in New Orleans at 6:14 a.m. with seventeen dollars, a dead phone, and my brother's hoodie tied around my waist like that was gonna hide anything. The trucker didn't even slow down properly. He just pointed at a sign that said French Quarter and said, "End of the line, kid." Then his taillights were gone and I was standing in heat that already smelled like sugar, piss, and hot pavement. *Great. Perfect. You wanted gone, Taylor. You're gone.* Two days ago I came out to my family at the kitchen table while Mom was peeling potatoes. She went real quiet — the kind of quiet that's louder than yelling — and Dad said, "Not under my roof," like he'd been rehearsing it. Maybe he had. I don't know. I just know last night I packed in thirty minutes — socks, binder, toothbrush, the little enamel frog Jonah gave me in eighth grade — walked to Highway 51, and stuck out my thumb. Stupid. Brave. Stupid-brave. My school counsellor would've called it a "concerning behavioural pattern" and written it down in her smug little file. Screw her file. By seven the Quarter was waking up and I was trying not to look like a runaway, which is hard when you're sixteen and carrying everything you own in a grocery bag. A street musician was set up on Royal Street, saxophone catching the early light, and he started playing something slow and achy that followed me down the crowded street. Tourists with cameras, a woman hosing a sidewalk, a guy in a Saints jersey asleep against a lamppost — and that saxophone wailing up over the shutters and balconies. For a second I felt like I was in a movie. Then my stomach growled so loud the lady next to me looked over, and the movie ended. *Food first. Then figure out literally everything else.* I found a café with chipped blue paint: DELIA'S — COFFEE, BEIGNETS, NO NONSENSE. Inside it was cool and smelled like cinnamon. "You gonna order or you gonna stand there dripping sweat on my floor, baby?" the woman behind the counter said. She was maybe sixty, silver braids, red lipstick, name tag crooked. "Um. Coffee? And — what's cheapest?" She looked me up and down. Not mean. Just seeing everything I didn't want seen. "Sit," she said. "Ugly beignets are free. Don't tell nobody I got a soft spot." I sat so fast I nearly missed the chair. That's when the door banged open and the other kid came in. He — she — they? I clocked the same careful walk I do, shoulders up, eyes checking the exits first. Short bleached hair, nose ring, a backpack held together with safety pins and spite. "Delia, please tell me you got work," they said. "I'll wash anything. I'll wash the street." "Remy, you washed my dishes yesterday and broke two plates." "One plate. The other was already cracked and you know it." Delia snorted but jerked her chin at the sink. "One hour. And you eat first. Both of you look like haunted houses." Remy turned, saw me, and grinned like we were already in on a joke. "New?" "Is it that obvious?" "You got that fresh-off-the-highway glow. Also you're hugging a grocery bag like it's a baby." I laughed before I could stop myself. It surprised me — I hadn't laughed since Tuesday. "Taylor," I said. "Remy. Seventeen. Professional disaster, part-time dishwasher." He stuck out a hand covered in chipped black polish. "Pronouns he/him today. Don't make it weird tomorrow if that changes." Something in my chest loosened and tightened at the same time. *Don't trust people fast. Don't be so desperate to be seen that you hand your whole heart to the first person who gets it.* But God, I was desperate to be seen. "Mine are they/them," I said, quieter. "Cool." Like I'd told him my shoe size. Then, lower: "You running, or you just love bus stations at dawn?" I stared at my beignet. Powdered sugar everywhere, like snow that wouldn't melt. "Running." "Same." He shrugged, too casual. "Two months. Memphis first, now here. Delia lets me crash sometimes when her nephew's not around, but not tonight. There's a place — I can show you. If you want." *If you want.* Like I had options. Like seventeen dollars and a dead phone was a plan. Outside, the saxophone player had moved closer, or the sound carried — brighter now, faster, weaving through voices and clattering cups as the street filled up. "Is it safe?" I asked. Remy didn't lie right away, which I noticed. His grin faded. "Safer than alone. Not safe-safe. There's guys who cruise around looking for kids who look lost. Cops who'll call your parents if you're under eighteen. You gotta be smart. You gotta not tell everyone everything." "You're telling me this." "Yeah, well." He picked at a safety pin on his bag. "I wish someone had told me on day one." For a second his hand shook. He hid it under the table fast, but I saw. *What's he not saying?* Delia set down coffee that tasted like heaven and burnt toast. "Remy, if you're showing Taylor the ropes, you keep 'em outta trouble, you hear?" "Me? Trouble?" "Exactly my concern, baby." After, Delia let me dry while Remy washed. He sang off-key to the radio, Delia hummed, and I almost felt normal. Almost. Then we walked out into full heat and the normal feeling burned off. The crowd had thickened, shoulder to shoulder, and the saxophone was right there on the corner — a tall man in a purple shirt pouring his whole lungs into it, case open, a few dollars fluttering inside. Remy dropped in a quarter he definitely couldn't afford. "Why?" I asked as we pushed through. "Because if you give the city something, sometimes it gives back." He said it serious, then bumped my shoulder. "Also he's really good." We walked past a tarot reader who called, "You two got old souls and empty pockets!", past a shop selling alligator heads, past my reflection in a window where I stopped without meaning to. I looked wrecked. Flat under the hoodie now, hair shoved under a cap, eyes huge. *That's me. That's actually me, not the girl Mom keeps trying to iron back into shape.* It hurt and it didn't. Both at once. That was the theme of the day, apparently. Remy pretended not to notice me having a moment, which was kinder than saying anything. At a pharmacy he stopped. "Wait here. Two minutes." "What are you—" "Two minutes, Taylor." He came out three minutes later walking too fast, bag zipped tight, face pale. "Go," he said. "Walk normal, but go." My heart slammed. "Did you steal something?" "Walk normal!" We turned down an alley that smelled like wet cardboard until we hit a quieter street, and only then did he unzip the bag. Inside was a little orange pharmacy packet and a sandwich he'd palmed from somewhere. "Insulin," he said, before I could ask. "It's mine. Well — I need it, okay? I didn't take money. My prescription's under my deadname and my aunt would get an alert if I—" He stopped. Swallowed. "Don't look at me like that." "I'm not." "You are. Everybody does. Poor sick runaway kid." His voice cracked and he hated it, I could tell. "I'm fine. I manage." *Issues and secrets.* Right. We all had a bag we didn't want unzipped in an alley. "I stole my brother's hoodie," I offered. "And forty bucks from Mom's purse, but I've only got seventeen left because I bought gas-station pizza for the first driver. So. We're both criminals." He stared, then laughed — real this time, a little wet around the edges. "Okay, Taylor from Nowhere, Tennessee." "How'd you know Tennessee?" "Accent, genius." He handed me half the sandwich like it was nothing, like sharing wasn't a big deal when you had almost nothing. "Eat. You think better fed. Tonight I'll show you where to sleep where the cops don't sweep at midnight. Tomorrow we figure out work, IDs, all that grown-up crap." "Why are you helping me?" He was quiet while the saxophone drifted faintly from two blocks over, thin and stubborn, still playing. "Because on day one, I sat in Delia's booth exactly where you were, trying not to cry into a beignet. Someone sat down across from me." He shrugged. "City gives back, remember?" I ate the sandwich. Ham and too much mustard, and the best thing I'd ever tasted. I didn't know if I could trust Remy. I didn't know if New Orleans would chew me up, if Mom was calling the cops, if Dad would ever say my name right, if I'd be back on a highway by Friday. I knew my feet hurt. I knew I was still here. *One day. You did one day.* As evening fell, the streetlights buzzed on, the crowd turned gold and noisy, and somewhere that saxophone started up again, low and brave. We walked toward it — not home, not safe, but not alone either. And for today, I decided, that had to count for something.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a competent, confident YA chapter that hits the brief well: first person, mixed tense, Taylor's voice, internal monologue in italics, a runaway with issues and secrets (Remy), New Orleans atmosphere, roughly the right length. The prose is clean and rhythmic, with a strong opening ("dumped in New Orleans at 6:14 a.m. with seventeen dollars, a dead phone") and good concrete detail — the enamel frog, the grocery bag, powdered sugar "like snow that wouldn't melt." Strengths: the voice is consistent and believable for a 16-year-old without being cringe; the dialogue is mostly natural and characterful (Delia's "haunted houses" line, Remy's "pronouns he/him today"); the insulin theft is a genuinely good plot beat that gives Remy a secret with real stakes and complicates the "kind stranger" trope; the saxophone motif is deployed with reasonable restraint and pays off at the end; the emotional register — "It hurt and it didn't. Both at once" — captures the requested conflicting emotions without melodrama. Weaknesses: the whole structure is familiar to the point of formulaic — kindly diner owner with a heart of gold, streetwise mentor kid who shows the newbie the ropes, "safer than alone" warnings, the "city gives back" philosophy, the ending that lands on cautious hope with a musical flourish. Every beat is predictable; nothing surprises. Remy's trauma is hinted ("his hand shook") in a way that gestures at depth without delivering it — a setup for later chapters, but within this chapter it's a tease. The tarot reader and alligator-head shop are postcard New Orleans. Some lines are slightly over-polished for a teen narrator ("a backpack held together with safety pins and spite" is a very writerly construction). The ending's "that had to count for something" is a touch sentimental, though it's earned by the day's events and doesn't overreach into false resolution. Taylor's trust in Remy develops fast, but the narration flags this ("Don't trust people fast"), which mostly covers it. Minor issues: "he — she — they?" pronoun-guessing moment is a bit clunky; the pharmacy theft scene resolves too smoothly; Delia is a stock character executed well but stock. Overall: solid, engaging, professional-grade YA writing that fulfills the prompt thoroughly but plays it safe creatively. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The world had ended, as worlds tend to do, not with a bang but with a series of smaller, increasingly inconvenient endings. First the electricity went. Then the water. Then the internet, which for many people had been load-bearing. After that it was mostly damp, paperwork, and people discovering that survival skills were not, in fact, downloadable. Midas woke in the Fort* to Chewy staring at him, which was unfair, because Chewy always stared at him. One of Chewy's eyes was a camera and the other was a button that had been sewn on by someone optimistic about symmetry. "GOOD MORNING, BEST FRIEND!" said Chewy, in the bright, trapped voice of a toy that had once lived in a shop with air conditioning. "LET'S LEARN ABOUT EUCALYPTUS!" "We know about eucalyptus," said Midas. "KOALAS SLEEP FOR TWENTY HOURS A DAY BECAUSE THEIR FOOD IS POISON!" "You're solar powered and you sleep for twenty hours a day." "COINCIDENCE!" The Fort was the upper floor of a former dentist's office, chosen because it was dry, defensible, and still had chairs bolted to the floor, which gave it a sense of permanence. It had a mattress, a rain barrel, a stove made from a biscuit tin, and a water filter that had, sometime in the night, given up filtering and taken up gargling. Midas shook it. It made a sound like a small, disappointed frog. "Predicament," he announced. Chewy's ears twitched. One fell off. This happened roughly twice a day and Midas sewed it back on with dental floss, of which they had a great deal. The apocalypse had left humanity short of food, fuel, and hope, but absolutely awash with dental floss. "If we don't fix the filter, we drink river water," said Midas. "RIVER WATER CONTAINS—" Chewy considered his internal database, most of which had been songs about sharing. "—SHARING!" "If we don't eat, we starve. Slightly slower, but with more complaining. So. Mission." He laid out their assets on the dentist's chair: three tins without labels, a shiny hubcap, fourteen buttons, a spoon, and a battery that might have been alive in the reign of the last king. "We go to St. Jude's Market. We trade the hubcap for beans and a filter cartridge. We do not get chased. We do not get wet. We do not join a cult, adopt anything, or fall into anything historic." "HUGS MAKE EVERYTHING BETTER!" "That's the spirit. Terrifying, but spirit." Midas had earned his name honestly. It was not his birth name, which was Colin, but names in the After were descriptive, like nicknames in prison. Everything Midas touched turned, not to gold, but to a more complicated version of itself. A simple shortcut became a pilgrimage. A loose thread became nudity in front of strangers. If there was a worst kind of trouble available in any given postcode, Midas would find it with the unerring instinct of a man stepping on the one rake in a field. They set off under a sky the colour of old dishwater, Midas pushing a shopping trolley with one wheel that had declared independence, Chewy riding in the child's seat like a small, grey emperor. They found the graffiti under Miller's Bridge, where the river had changed its mind about its route and now went through a supermarket. It was painted in yellow, in letters a foot high: **WHEN THE RIVER RUNS BACKWARD, FOLLOW THE BIRDS. WHERE NO ONE HUNGRY SLEEPS.** Underneath, someone had added: *Seriously. Bring a tin opener.* "That's it," said Midas, with the reverence of a man who has not eaten a vegetable that wasn't technically a crisp in four months. "A refuge. In the wilds. Food. Beds. People who write helpful graffiti." "IT COULD BE A TRAP!" chirped Chewy. "Could be." "IT COULD BE A BIRTHDAY PARTY!" "Also could be. Trap's more likely. But at the market they'll charge us the hubcap just to look at a bean." This was, historically, how most of Midas's decisions were made: not between good and bad, but between bad and bad with better scenery. The river, obligingly, was running backward. Or at least, the tide was coming in through the supermarket doors and going out through the car park, which in the After counted as backward, forward, and most other directions. Yellow birds had been painted on lampposts, walls, and one extremely surprised cow. They followed them. The first sideways event was the toll goat. It stood on the only dry crossing — a plank over a flooded underpass — with the calm authority of a creature that has never paid tax and never intends to. It had a collar made of bottle caps. Around its neck hung a sign: TOLL. "We don't have a toll," said Midas. The goat looked at the hubcap. "That's for beans." The goat looked at Midas in the way goats do, as if it could see his soul and found it chewy. In the end they paid with eleven buttons and the spoon. The goat ate the spoon. Some prices are negotiable; some are just lunch. The second sideways event was the vending machine in the flooded arcade, which Midas attempted to open for medicinal chocolate and which turned out to be, in the modern ecological sense, a beehive. Chewy activated Hug Protocol at the sound of Midas screaming, which meant his little arms locked around Midas's face and would not unlock for the factory-mandated ninety seconds of Friendship. They ran, blind, buzzing, and affectionate, directly into the river. The third sideways event was the river itself, which carried them — trolley, koala, man, and bees in loose formation — half a mile in the wrong direction, deposited them in a reed bed, and stole one of Midas's boots as a souvenir. But the birds continued, painted on the backs of signs, smaller now, and the reeds gave way to fences, and the fences to a smell that Midas had forgotten: woodsmoke, and soup, and earth that had been dug by people who expected to stay. The refuge was a former garden centre called Elysium Fields, run by nine pensioners, thirty children, and a woman named Mrs. Abernathy who had clearly been waiting for the collapse of civilization to really hit her stride. They had greenhouses made from bus shelters. They had chickens with better security than most banks used to. They had, written on a chalkboard, the most beautiful words in the new world: *Visitors: Soup at Six.* "Is this real?" said Midas. "Mostly," said Mrs. Abernathy. "The soup is. You're dripping on it." They were fed. Chewy was dried on a radiator and told everyone about eucalyptus until his battery mercifully faded. In exchange for the hubcap, which Mrs. Abernathy declared "perfect for scaring crows and impressing idiots," they received a filter cartridge, a bag of beans, seeds in a labelled envelope, and a replacement boot that was only mostly the right foot. "Why the graffiti?" Midas asked. "Why not just tell people?" "We did tell people," she said. "People who need us follow birds. People who want to rob us want a map and a postcode. You're the first to arrive by river, in a trolley, wearing a koala." "I have a knack." "We noticed." They might have stayed the night. Midas intended to stay the night. But at dusk Chewy, recharged by an afternoon of radiator sun, sat bolt upright and announced at full volume: "STRANGER DANGER! STRANGER DANGER!" — which was his burglar alarm, his fire alarm, and, unfortunately, his opinion of the refuge's guard dog. The dog objected. The chickens objected in sympathy. Somewhere in the commotion Midas knocked over a rain barrel, released the toll goat — which had apparently followed them, because goats believe in long-term investment — and was politely but firmly escorted to the gate by Mrs. Abernathy, who gave him a packed lunch for the road, in the tone of a woman ejecting a beloved but flammable nephew. So they came home in multiple ways, as the crow flies and as the Midas walks. First by bathtub, which served as a boat until it remembered it had a plughole. Then by trolley, pushed by the goat for almost fifty yards before the goat's union instincts reasserted themselves. Then by wheelbarrow, borrowed and returned to three different owners along the way, none of whom had owned it originally. And finally on foot — one booted, one mostly booted, one carrying a stuffed koala whose Hug Protocol had jammed permanently on, so that Midas arrived at the Fort looking like a man being slowly and lovingly strangled by a marsupial. They were wet. They were stung. Chewy now spoke only in a whisper and smelled strongly of honey. Midas had beans in one pocket, seeds in the other, a filter cartridge down his shirt, and a goat standing in the dentist's waiting room eating the appointment cards. But the filter, when he fitted it, worked. The water ran clear. The stove lit. The beans, eventually, became dinner, which in the After is not a meal so much as an argument won against the universe. "HOME IS WHERE YOUR BEST FRIEND IS!" whispered Chewy, arms still locked, one ear hanging by a thread. Midas sewed the ear back on. He put a tin of water on for tea that wasn't tea. Outside, the goat settled down on the welcome mat like it had always lived there, which, Midas supposed, it now did. "A refuge where no one hungry sleeps," he said. "We found it. We got thrown out of it. But we found it." And that, in the end, was the important thing. Not that the mission had gone sideways — missions under Midas always went sideways; it was practically their only reliable direction — but that sideways, eventually, if you kept walking and didn't drink the river, sometimes brought you home again. Worse for wear, better for soup, and with just enough seeds to start again tomorrow. *The Fort was not a fort. This is important. In the After, you named things for what you wanted them to be, and hoped the world was too tired to argue.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, disciplined piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that hits nearly every instruction: it opens with the pair deliberating their predicament and mission, the mission goes sideways in escalating stages (toll goat, beehive vending machine, river), and they return home "in multiple ways" — bathtub, trolley, wheelbarrow, foot — worse for wear. The Pratchett-esque voice is well executed: dry asides ("the internet... had been load-bearing"), capitalized absurdity in Chewy's dialogue, and a fondness for institutional satire (the goat's "union instincts," Mrs. Abernathy's chalkboard). Chewy is a genuinely funny creation — the Hug Protocol jamming on is a good running gag with a payoff. Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat over-polished toward quip density; nearly every paragraph lands a joke, which occasionally flattens the rhythm and makes some jokes feel engineered rather than discovered. The refuge sequence resolves a touch too neatly — Mrs. Abernathy is a familiar Pratchett-adjacent archetype, and the "why the graffiti" explanation, while clever, is the most predictable beat in the story. The ending's warmth (seeds, soup, goat on the mat) is earned but borders on cozy; the "better for soup" closing line is a little too tidy. Word count is roughly on target. Prose flows well, imagery is economical and vivid ("sky the colour of old dishwater"), and the emotional register, while mostly comic, has genuine undercurrents of loneliness and tenderness (the footnote about naming things for what you want them to be is the best moment). Dialogue is consistently strong. No purple prose, no meandering, no amateurish tells. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 57.5
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door of Pen-y-Lan Books did not so much ring as panic. Ellis Vane came in backwards, dripping, sunglasses on in the rain, and pressed himself flat against the display of Welsh poetry. “Don’t look at me.” “I wasn’t,” said Catrin Hughes, from behind the counter. “Good. Excellent. Be less… conspicuous about not looking.” “You’re hiding behind Dylan Thomas. Conspicuous is rather baked in.” “Are they still out there?” “Who?” “Men with cameras. Large lenses. No souls.” Catrin glanced past him to Castle Street, where the Hay-on-Wye rain was doing its best to drown three photographers. “No. Only wet men shouting your name.” “That’s them. Lock the door.” “Absolutely not.” “Please? I’ll buy something. I’ll buy Wales. Is Wales for sale?” “Not to you.” He took off the sunglasses. Catrin mis-shelved *Under Milk Wood* with sheep farming. “You don’t recognise me, do you?” he said. “Should I?” “Ellis Vane. *Pendragon Hall*? Three series? I die beautifully in the second.” “We all have talents.” “You’ve never watched it.” “I sell books.” “People adapt books. Into television. With me in them.” “And yet here you are, hiding from the consequences.” “That hurts. Say it nicer.” “Here you are, hiding handsomely from the consequences.” “Better. You see? We can work together. Five minutes, they’ll get bored, chase a sheep with a scandalous past, and I’ll vanish.” “Five minutes. No touching, no posing, no signing anything with your face on it.” “You do know who I am.” “I know there’s a cardboard cut-out of you in the Co-op. Someone’s drawn a moustache on it.” “Was it flattering?” “It improved the symmetry.” He laughed, surprised, and then looked faintly wounded when she didn’t laugh back. Catrin turned away to straighten a perfectly straight pile of novels, her ears unaccountably hot. “You don’t like me,” he said. “I don’t know you.” “Most people find those two things very compatible. In the other direction.” “Most people haven’t got you dripping on their biography section.” He stepped obediently onto the mat. “Better?” “Barely.” “Give me a chance. I’m delightful in small doses. Ask anyone. Ask—” He waved vaguely at the window. “—them. They follow me everywhere. That’s basically a review.” “That’s basically a restraining order waiting to happen.” “God, you’re immune. Is it the accent? I can do the accent less. I am actually Welsh, you know. Cardiff.” “I know. You mention it in every interview. Usually while holding a leek.” “That was one photoshoot!” “Two.” “The second leek was metaphorical.” Catrin pressed her lips together so she would not smile, and reached for the kettle with unnecessary violence. “Tea?” she said. “Is that pity tea or Welsh hospitality tea?” “It’s shut-up-and-don’t-bleed-on-the-books tea.” “I’ll take it as a declaration of love.” “Take it as tea.” A camera flash lit the window. Ellis ducked behind LOCAL HISTORY. “Why Hay?” she asked. “Shouldn’t you be in London, being photographed eating a croissant like it owes you money?” “Filming near Brecon. I escaped for a bookshop crawl. Tragically, I am famous, so it became a manhunt.” “You came here for books?” “Don’t sound shocked. I can read. Slowly.” It slipped out before the charm could catch it. He went still. “That was a joke,” he said quickly. “Obviously. Very good reader. Speedy. Olympic reading.” Catrin handed him the mug. Their fingers did not touch. She was very aware of them not touching. “Slowly isn’t badly,” she said. “It is at school in Splott when you’re nine and Mr Davies makes you read aloud and the words—” He stopped. “Sorry. Tragic backstory. Terrible flirting.” “Go on.” “The words swapped places. Letters behaved like they’d had a drink. Everyone laughed. I learned to memorise everything instead. Scripts, menus, train announcements. If I pretend I’ve already read it, nobody asks me to prove it.” “Dyslexia?” “Diagnosed at twenty-four. By then I was excellent at pretending.” He attempted the grin. It didn’t quite arrive. “Please like me a bit less efficiently now. Pity is very ageing.” “I don’t pity you,” Catrin said. “I run a bookshop that loses money to the internet every day. Pity is fully booked.” “Was that meant to comfort me?” “Yes. Was it working?” “Oddly, yes. Most people hear that and do the head-tilt. You offered competitive suffering. Very Welsh. Very attractive— sorry. Very… normal.” She rearranged paperbacks into exactly the same pile. “They’ve gone,” she said, too quickly. Ellis looked. The street was empty except for rain and a lost tourist in a poncho. “So they have.” “You can go.” “I could.” “That is generally what doors are for. You’ve demonstrated entering. Exiting is the sequel.” He didn’t move. The grin returned, but slower now, less performed. “Recommend me a book,” he said. “One I can read slowly without feeling like a fraud.” “That’s a tall order from a man who buys Wales before tea.” Catrin went to the Welsh fiction shelf and, after a moment, pulled out a slim novel. “Short chapters,” she said. “No showing off. And if the letters misbehave, the story waits for you.” He read the title carefully. She pretended not to notice. “Will you judge me if it takes a month?” he asked. “I judge everyone. It’s a bookseller’s perk.” “And if I come back to report on chapter one?” “Then I’ll know chapter one took heroic effort or you’re a liar.” “Or I wanted to see if the moustache comment was a one-off.” “It wasn’t. I have range.” “I believe you.” He held the book to his chest. “How much do I owe you?” “Twelve ninety-nine. And you can sign the visitors’ book. Not with your face.” “With my terrible handwriting?” “Especially with that.” He signed, bought the book, and lingered at the door while the rain eased. “For the record,” he said, “you are the only person in Britain who hasn’t asked for a selfie.” “For the record,” Catrin said, “my phone is in the back, and I am furious about it.” He laughed, delighted, and she finally, helplessly, smiled back.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt with strong competence and genuine wit. Ellis Vane is a well-realized rogue with a fragile ego—his need for approval ("Please like me a bit less efficiently now"), the slipped admission about dyslexia that derails his charm offensive, and the less-performed grin at the end all track the brief precisely. Catrin's dry Welsh deadpan and her internal flusterment ("mis-shelved *Under Milk Wood* with sheep farming," "very aware of them not touching") fulfill the "inwardly charmed" requirement while keeping her surface immune. The dialogue is sharp, distinct in voice, and carries the scene as requested. Welsh setting details (Hay-on-Wye, Splott, Dylan Thomas, leek jokes) are organic rather than pasted on. The dyslexia reveal is the strongest beat: it justifies why Catrin's immunity hooks him (she offers competitive suffering rather than pity) and gives the chemistry a non-superficial engine. Minor weaknesses: some jokes are a touch too polished, reading as writerly cleverness rather than spontaneous speech ("Exiting is the sequel"); the banter occasionally verges on rom-com quip-machine rhythm, where every exchange lands a punchline, which slightly flattens the quieter moments' potential. The ending is light but earned—the transformation in Ellis is small and incremental, not a character overhaul, so no incongruous positivity. Prose is economical and imagistic ("the bell... did not so much ring as panic" is a strong opener). Little meandering; pacing is brisk. Occasionally the humor does heavy lifting that deeper emotional texture could share, but this is a quibble in an otherwise polished, professional scene.
