+ Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 75.9
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Rewind Watch ## Chapter 7 The first time it happened, I thought I was losing my mind. The second time, I thought I was lucky. By the fifth time, the cat was waiting for me. Not just any cat. The scrawny orange stray that lived behind the dumpsters at Shady Valley Middle School. One green eye. One blue eye. A torn left ear. Every time I came back, it was there. Sitting perfectly still. Staring at me. Not at my face, exactly. At my watch. Then at my face again, like it was comparing the two. Like it *remembered* me from before. Which was impossible. Because before hadn't happened anymore. At least, not for anyone else. My name is Jordan Ellis. I'm twelve years old. Or I was, last Tuesday, when Mom gave me the watch for my birthday. It wasn't even a real brand name. Just a black smart watch in a silver box with no instructions. Mom said Aunt Carla found it at an estate sale and thought it looked "futuristic." It told the time. It counted my steps. And at 12:07 in the cafeteria, when I tripped in front of the entire seventh grade and sent chocolate milk flying all over Mia Torres's white sweater, it did something else. I grabbed the watch while everyone was laughing. I squeezed the little dial on the side and thought, *I wish I could do that over.* The world made a sound like a tape rewinding. *Zzzzip!* The laughing stopped. The milk was back in my carton. Mia's sweater was clean. My watch said 12:02. Five minutes earlier. Nobody else noticed. Nobody except the orange cat outside the cafeteria window, staring in at me with its head tilted. I didn't trip the second time. After that, it was so easy. Forgot to study for a science quiz? *Zzzzip.* Back to breakfast. I studied while eating my toast. Said something totally embarrassing to my best friend Sam? *Zzzzip.* Conversation erased. Missed the winning shot in gym? *Zzzzip.* I took it again, and made it. Each time, the cat was there. After the quiz, it was by the bike racks. After gym, it was on the fence by the field, licking one paw, watching me. Its blue eye blinked. Then its green eye. Slowly. Like a warning. I ignored it. Why wouldn't I? I had a superpower. Only... my shoes started hurting. Not a little. A lot. My toes smashed against the front by Thursday. My jeans, which Mom had just bought, stopped above my ankles. "You had a growth spurt," Mom said at dinner, smiling. "Pass the potatoes, honey." But my voice cracked when I said, "Okay." Deep, then squeaky, then deep again. Dad laughed. "Whoa! Puberty hits fast, huh, champ?" Everyone laughed. I laughed too, but my stomach went cold. Because the next morning, there was a pimple on my forehead the size of a marble. My sleeves were too short. My favorite t-shirt, the one with the dinosaur on it, fit like it belonged to a little kid. And it hit me, standing in the bathroom: I wasn't just rewinding time. Time was taking it back. From *me*. Five minutes here. Twenty minutes there. An hour for the math test. Every minute I went back, my body jumped forward. Weeks. Maybe months. I tried to take the watch off. The strap wouldn't open. It wasn't stuck. It was... tighter. Like it had grown into my wrist. The screen lit up all by itself: **BALANCE DUE** Then it went black. That's when I should have stopped. But Friday, I gave my book report in English, and I completely froze. I forgot the author's name. I forgot the book's name. Kids started snickering. Mr. Lopez said, "Jordan? We're waiting," in that voice teachers use when they're disappointed in you. My face burned. My hands shook. So under my desk, I pressed the dial and held it. And held it. And held it. *Take me back to this morning,* I thought. *All the way back.* The rewind sound screamed in my ears. The classroom stretched like taffy. Colors smeared. My stomach flipped over and over — *ZZZZIP!* I woke up in bed. My alarm said 7:00 a.m. Friday morning. I did it! I had the whole day to redo! Then I sat up, and my feet touched the floor way too fast. My legs were longer. I ran to the bathroom mirror and nearly screamed. The face looking back wasn't twelve. It was older. Maybe fifteen. Maybe sixteen. My jaw was sharper. My forehead was broken out. There was a scratchy shadow over my upper lip, and when I said, "No, no, no," my voice was *deep*. Completely deep. No crack at all. "Jordan! You're going to be late for school!" Mom called. "And remember, you promised you'd drive Sam to practice after!" Drive? I stumbled into the hall. The family photos had changed. There I was at the beach last summer — taller than Mom. There I was holding a learner's permit, grinning. There I was on a high school football team I had never joined. Downstairs, Sam was eating cereal at our table. My best friend since kindergarten. He looked exactly the same. Twelve. Small. He looked up at me and went a little pale. "Uh... hi," he said. Like I was a stranger. Like I was a *grown-up*. "Mom said you have to take me because you're the only one with a license. You don't have to be mad." "Sam, it's me," I whispered. "We had a sleepover last Saturday. We built the fort—" He frowned. "That was when we were kids. You don't hang out with me anymore. You said I'm too immature." My heart hammered against my ribs. The timeline hadn't just changed my body. It had changed *everything else* to match. My life had been rewritten around my new age. Friends. Photos. Memories that everyone had except me. Outside the kitchen window, something scratched the glass. The orange cat. It was sitting on the fence, in the rain that hadn't been falling a minute ago, staring straight at me. It didn't blink this time. It lifted one paw and pressed it against the window, right toward my watch. And for the first time, I understood. It wasn't recognizing me. It was trying to warn me. It was the only one whose time hadn't been rewritten. The only one who remembered the real me, every single version. My watch buzzed against my skin. Hot. **ONE CORRECTION REMAINING** I knew what I had to do. Rewind again. All the way back to Tuesday morning, before Mom gave me the box. Before I ever put it on. If I could get there, maybe I could refuse it. Smash it. Bury it. Maybe everything would snap back. Or maybe — and this thought made my hands go ice-cold — maybe the price for going back three whole days would be years. Three years. Five years. Ten. The cat shook its head, just once. Very slowly. Very human. "No choice," I told it. My deep, stranger's voice shook. "I have to try." I grabbed the dial. The cat yowled. I pressed it down and thought of Tuesday, of birthday candles, of being twelve — And the last thing I saw before the world ripped backward was my hand on the watch. It was covered in dark hair. The fingers were long and thick. A man's hand. And it was still getting older.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent Goosebumps-style middle-grade horror chapter that hits nearly all prompt requirements: smart watch rewind mechanic, aging cost, puberty acceleration, social changes, timeline shift, cliffhanger reversal. The prose is punchy and age-appropriate, with short paragraphs and a strong hook (the cat). The cat as a time-immune witness is a nice touch, though it borders on convenient. The escalation is well-paced: small rewinds, physical signs, the "BALANCE DUE" screen, then the catastrophic full-day rewind. The ending cliffhanger with the man's hand is effective. Weaknesses: some clichés (chocolate milk spill, growth spurt dialogue), the "drive Sam" plot hole (a 15-16 year old with a license after skipping ~3-4 years is plausible but rushed), and the mechanic of "everyone's memories rewritten" is asserted rather than fully dramatized. Dialogue is serviceable but thin. Some telling ("I understood," "my heart hammered"). The voice is consistent first-person, appropriately juvenile. Emotionally engaging but not deeply complex — fear and dread, little else. The "maybe?" ambiguity of the fix is preserved well. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 85.7
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk in Coney Island, July 1937, and the air still held the day's heat — salt and hot oil and sugar from the taffy stands, the ocean breathing somewhere beyond the planks. The Cyclone clattered overhead and somebody screamed, delighted, as the cars dropped. Around her, girls in summer dresses clung to boys in shirtsleeves, and the boardwalk's sodium lights flickered inconsistently, buzzing, going amber, then white, then amber again, casting strange patterns on the strangers' faces. *His locks.* The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase, and something else with it — dangerously compelling — quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. She had told Walter she was visiting her cousin in Bay Ridge. She had taken the train the other way. He was already there. He leaned against the counter of the gallery as if he owned no part of it and all of it at once, sleeves rolled to the elbow, a cigarette unlit behind his ear. The young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. "You came back," he said. "I was passing," she said. "From Bay Ridge?" Her heart misbehaved. "I didn't say I was in Bay Ridge." "You didn't have to." He straightened, slow. "You left this yesterday." From his pocket he drew her handkerchief. Linen. Her initials, embroidered by her mother in pale blue: *E.M.* "You kept it." "I meant to return it." "All night?" "I had to be sure you'd come for it." "I've come for it now." She held out her hand. "Thank you." He did not give it to her. "E. M." "Give it to me, please." "Tell me what it stands for." "That isn't necessary." "Eleanor? Edith? Eve?" "No." "Eve would suit you." "I'm engaged to be married," she said, too quickly. "I saw the ring yesterday. I see you're turning it round and round now." His gaze dropped, then lifted. "Does he know you come to Coney Island alone?" "He knows I enjoy the sea air." "Is that what you call this? Sea air?" The light above the gallery stuttered. For a second his face was all shadow and cheekbone, a stranger in a penny dreadful. Then it cleared, and he was only a man, perhaps twenty-eight, watching her too closely. *Go home, Evelyn. Take the handkerchief and go home and marry Walter and live in a clean apartment in Queens and never think of this man's mouth again.* "Mrs. — Miss — M.," the barker called to someone else, "three shots, a nickel, win the lady a doll!" "Give me my handkerchief," she said. "Win it." "I beg your pardon?" He nodded toward the row of chained rifles, the moving tin ducks painted yellow, their eyes chipped. "Three shots. Hit two and I'll give it back. And a prize besides." "And if I miss?" "Then you walk with me to the end of the pier. That's all." "That's not all and you know it." "Isn't it? What are you afraid will happen on a pier, in public, before nine o'clock?" "With you? I haven't decided." Something in his face changed — amusement, and respect for the answer. "Then shoot." "I don't shoot." "Everybody shoots. It's America." "I shouldn't be speaking to you at all." "Yet here we are. Speaking." He picked up a rifle and held it out, not by the barrel but by the stock, like an invitation. "Your fiancé teach you?" "Walter doesn't approve of carnivals." "Walter." He tasted the name and discarded it. "What does Walter approve of?" "Steady employment. A savings account. Church on Sunday." "A thrilling list." "Don't mock him. He's a good man." "I'm sure he is." The sodium light flickered again, striping his eyes. "Are you a good woman?" She took the rifle. It was heavier than she expected. "That is an impertinent question." "You took the gun instead of answering." "Load it, then, if you're so clever." He stepped closer. Not touching her — not quite — but close enough that she felt the heat of him through her dress, close enough to smell tobacco and bay rum and clean sweat. "Feet apart." "Excuse me?" "To shoot. Feet apart. Like this." He waited until she obeyed. "Shoulder up. Cheek here. Don't close your eyes." "I'm not a child." "No," he said quietly. "That's the difficulty." His hand came to her wrist to steady it. Only his fingers. Only for a moment longer than necessary. She felt the callus on his thumb against her pulse. *If Walter touched me like that I would call it improper. If this man stops, I will call it a disappointment, and what does that make me?* "Now," he said. "That duck. The ugly one." "They're all ugly." "Pick the one you hate most. It helps." She fired. The cork cracked and a duck two places from hers tipped over. "I hit one." "You hit his neighbor. In Brooklyn that's still a scandal." Despite herself, she laughed. "You're terrible." "You've noticed." He reloaded for her, deft. "Again." "People are looking." "Let them. They think I'm teaching my girl to shoot." "I'm not your girl." "No? Then why did you dream—" "I did not—" She stopped. His voice lowered. "You were going to lie very prettily. Don't. Not about that." "I don't know you," she whispered. "You know enough to come back." "I know nothing. Not even your name." "Ask me." "I won't give you the satisfaction." "Then I'll keep the handkerchief. A man needs something to remember a lady by when she marries her savings account." "That was cruel." "It was meant to be. You're wasting something, Evelyn." She went still. "How—" "The M is for May. Evelyn May. It was on the tag inside your glove, too. You left that yesterday as well, in your hurry to run from me." "I didn't run." "You did. Very fast. In very impractical shoes." He produced the glove now, too, and laid it on the counter between them like evidence. "You wanted a reason to return. I am obliging enough to provide two." The Cyclone roared again. Somewhere a child cried for cotton candy. The gallery lights hummed and failed and hummed, making his curls black, then brown, then black. "Last shot," he said. "Hit it clean and you take both, and your prize, and you go back to Walter with a clear conscience." "And if I miss again?" "The pier. One walk. You can tell me all about steady employment, and I will try not to fall asleep." "And after the pier?" "After the pier you decide." "Decide what?" "Whether you're as good as you keep insisting." She raised the rifle. Her hands were not steady, and not from the weight. She was aware of her stocking seams, her lipstick, the ring biting as she curled her finger. She was aware of him not touching her now, which was somehow worse. She fired. The duck fell cleanly. The barker whistled. "Winner! Lady wins! Take the doll, take the kewpie, take the painted rose — what'll it be, sweetheart?" She did not look at the prizes. She looked at him. He returned the handkerchief and the glove, placing them in her palm and closing her fingers over them himself. "Well shot." "Thank you." "You're free to go." "I know I am." "Then go." She did not move. The lights flickered inconsistently overhead, casting strange patterns — half his face in gold, half in darkness. "Tomorrow," he said at last, as if it cost him something to be the one to say it, "they close the gallery at eleven. The man lets me keep the key a little after." "Why are you telling me?" "Because you didn't go." He stepped back, putting the counter between them again, a deliberate mercy. "Behind the gallery. If you want your third thing." "I left only two things." "I know," he said. "Come and find out what it is." She walked away without answering, the kewpie doll ridiculous in her arms, the boardwalk tilting under her impractical shoes. *I will not come,* she told herself, all the way to the train. *I will not, I will not.* She was still telling herself at midnight, wide awake beside the window, already deciding what dress to wear.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This scene is a strong piece of period romantic tension writing that fulfills the brief with considerable skill. The 1937 Coney Island setting is rendered with economical, sensory detail — salt, hot oil, taffy, the Cyclone screaming overhead, the flickering sodium lights that do real atmospheric work by repeatedly half-erasing and revealing the stranger's face. The lights become a motif of moral ambiguity, casting the man alternately as stranger and suitor, which is exactly the "romantic allure with an undercurrent of danger" the prompt requested. The dialogue is the piece's chief strength. It crackles with period-appropriate repartee: "Then you walk with me to the end of the pier. That's all." / "That's not all and you know it." The handkerchief and glove as tokens/reasons-to-return is a well-chosen device — it gives the woman agency in her own transgression while letting the man remain ambiguous rather than predatory. His knowing her name from the glove tag flirts with surveillance-creepiness, but the story acknowledges this ("I don't know you," she whispered) and the woman's irritation keeps it in tension rather than romance-by-default. Lines like "Everybody shoots. It's America" and "In Brooklyn that's still a scandal" land as genuinely witty without breaking tone. The internal monologue is well-judged and sparse: "I will not, I will not" closing, and the sharp self-aware line "If this man stops, I will call it a disappointment, and what does that make me?" — this is the emotional complexity the prompt wanted, the feminine perspective rendered as complicity rather than victimhood. The proportions roughly match the requested 50/20/30 split. Weaknesses: the man occasionally verges on the too-scripted, fantasy-boyfriend archetype — always one beat ahead, never wrong, tasting "Walter" and discarding it. His omniscience about her (the glove tag, the impractical shoes) is charming but borders on implausible convenience. The woman's protests ("I'm not your girl," "I won't give you the satisfaction") follow a slightly predictable push-pull rhythm that a reader of this genre will recognize; the beats are well-executed but not surprising. The ending — her deciding what dress to wear — is the expected note, though it's earned by the preceding ambivalence. A few moments ("That's the difficulty") are a touch too neatly aphoristic. The prose is clean and controlled, never purple, though it occasionally reaches for the polished epigram over the true. Overall this is a confident, coherent, atmospheric scene with genuine tension and only minor formulaic tendencies. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Two** That night back at the lodge, everything was the way it always was, and that was somehow worse than if it hadn't been. His father fried steaks in the big iron skillet, the grease popping and spitting, while Mike set out tin plates and poured coffee so black it looked like used motor oil. The Coleman lantern hissed over the table. Outside, the wind worked at the shutters the way it always had, worrying the loose one over the bunkroom window — *tap, tap-tap, tap* — a sound JT had fallen asleep to since he was six years old. "You should've seen the one that got away from us, Junior," Mike said. JT looked up. "Yeah?" "Big bastard. Ten points, maybe twelve." Mike held his hands up beside his head, fingers spread, grinning. "Standing right there in Miller's Clearing like he owned the place. Wasn't that right, Dad?" His father didn't answer at first. He was turning a steak with a fork, watching the blood well up through the seared meat. "Right," he said at last. "Big one." "And Dad here forgot he was carrying a rifle." "I didn't forget." "No?" Mike laughed, but there was no real meanness in it. "Could've fooled me. You were just standing there with your mouth open. I swear, I thought you were gonna ask it to dance." His father smiled then, a thin, tired smile that didn't quite get to his eyes. "Must've been buck fever." "You? Buck fever? Since when?" "Since I got old, I guess." They ate. The steak was tough and good, salty at the edges. The beans were straight from the can. JT chewed and listened to the lantern hiss and tried to tell himself that was all it had been. Buck fever. A man in his fifties, a cold morning, a moment's hesitation. It happened. Everybody knew it happened. (*Only he hadn't hesitated, had he? Hesitating was something else. Hesitating was a man with his rifle halfway up, trying to decide. His father hadn't decided anything. His father had reached out like a man in church.*) "You quiet tonight," his father said. JT shrugged. "Tired." "He's always quiet," Mike said. "That's his whole personality. Isn't that right, Junior? Quiet and weird." "Shut up." "Make me." It was normal. It was so aggressively, insistently normal that JT felt something in his chest loosen and then, perversely, tighten again. Because if they could sit here and eat steak and talk like this, then maybe nothing *had* happened in the clearing. Maybe he'd been crouched behind that brush too long with the cold getting into his knees, imagining things. He was good at imagining things. His mother had said so, usually when a teacher called home. He didn't mention what he'd seen. He told himself it was because there was nothing to mention. The truth — and he knew it even then, the way you know a tooth is loose before you can bring yourself to touch it with your tongue — was that he was afraid of how his father might look at him if he did. Later, washing plates in the enamel basin, Mike said, "You want to try north of the lake tomorrow, Dad? Past the old Travers place?" His father went still. Not very still. Just still enough that JT noticed. "Nothing up there," he said. "There was last year. Eddie LaChance got a cow up there opening day." "Eddie LaChance would shoot his own shadow if you put antlers on it." "I'm just saying. Nobody's hunted it yet this season. Because of the stories, probably." Mike glanced at JT and waggled his eyebrows, putting on his spooky voice. "The man in the cabin. Oooooh." "Don't be an ass," his father said, without heat. "What man?" JT asked. Mike was delighted, the way he always was when he got to be the one who knew something. "The old Travers cabin. You know it. Past the lake, where the trail gives out. Been empty since before we were born — roof half caved, door hanging open. Only the old guys at the gas station say it isn't empty. Say in the off-season there's smoke from the chimney sometimes. Say somebody keeps a fire in there all winter, but there's never tracks in the snow. Never a truck. Nothing." "Somebody poaching and keeping his mouth shut," his father said. "That's all that is." "Sure. Or it's a ghost. Or a crazy hermit who eats hunters and uses their bones for wind chimes." Mike shrugged into his coat. "Everybody up here has a story about it. Nobody'll hunt past it, though. Funny, isn't it? Grown men with rifles, scared of an empty house." "It isn't empty," JT said. He hadn't meant to say it out loud. Both of them looked at him. "I mean — that's what people say, right? That it isn't." Mike laughed and clapped him on the shoulder hard enough to slosh the dishwater. "See? He's spooked already and we haven't even gone yet. We're going, Dad. I decided. North of the lake." His father dried his hands slowly on a rag that had once been a towel. He looked at the window, where his own reflection looked back, pale and doubled in the black glass. "Fine," he said. "Early, though. And we don't go in the cabin. There's no reason to go in the cabin." JT lay awake a long time that night listening to the loose shutter. *Tap, tap-tap, tap.* Somewhere in the middle of it he became convinced there was another sound underneath, keeping time with it — breathing, maybe, slow and deep, from the empty third bunk where nobody slept anymore. When he finally worked up the nerve to sit up and look, there was nothing there but Mike's spare coat thrown over the mattress. He told himself he hadn't really expected anything else. He almost believed it. --- They went north of the lake in a morning so cold the frost on the inside of the truck windows had to be scraped with a credit card. Nobody talked much. His father drove with both hands high on the wheel, the way he did when the road was bad, though the road wasn't bad. It was just empty, a long grey cut through spruce that all leaned the same way, like they'd been listening for something for a hundred years and had gotten stiff doing it. The Travers cabin sat where the trail gave out, exactly where JT remembered it from the one time he'd seen it as a little kid, and it was wrong in the same way the buck had been wrong. It looked abandoned. That wasn't the problem. The tarpaper roof sagged, one window was boarded, the door hung open on a single hinge, banging softly. It looked abandoned the way a held breath looks like rest. And there was smoke coming from the chimney. Not much. A thin blue thread of it, straight up into the windless air. "Dad," Mike said quietly. "I see it." "Poacher, right? Like you said." "Probably." "Should we — " "We don't go in the cabin," his father said. He said it to the windshield. His hands were still high on the wheel and JT could see, very clearly, that they were trembling again. "We hunt the ridge. That's all we came to do." They hunted the ridge. Or they walked it, anyway, rifles carried and not raised, for maybe an hour, in a silence that got heavier the longer nobody filled it. JT kept finding his eyes pulled back down the slope toward that thin line of smoke. Twice he thought he saw the cabin door swing shut. Twice, when he looked again, it was open. It was Mike who finally said it, of course. Mike, who couldn't leave anything alone. They had stopped to rest where the ridge fell away toward the trees, and the cabin was visible below them, small and dark, and Mike said, "I'm going down to look. Just to look. Five minutes." "Mike — " "Five minutes, Dad. If some guy's squatting in there I want to know before he puts a hole in one of us by accident." His father should have said no. JT waited for him to say no, and felt the whole morning tilt when he didn't. What his father said, in a voice JT had never heard him use before — soft, almost wondering — was: "I'll go." "Dad?" "You boys stay here." He went down the slope alone, rifle slung, hands empty at his sides, walking not like a man approaching a house but like a man who has heard his name called from inside one. JT watched him cross the little yard, where there were no tracks in the frost except the ones he was making. Watched him stop at the open door. Watched him raise one hand — slowly, fingers spread — and lay it flat against the doorframe, the way you'd touch the face of an animal to calm it. Then he stepped inside, and the door swung shut behind him without a sound. "Okay," Mike said. His voice had lost all its teasing. "Okay, that's — Dad? *Dad!*" Nothing. The smoke went up. The woods went on being quiet in that leaned-in way. JT was already moving. He didn't remember deciding to. He went down through the spruce with his rifle banging against his hip and his breath burning, and he came around the side of the cabin to the unboarded window, the one black square of glass, and he made himself look in. His father was kneeling in the middle of the floor. Just kneeling, head bowed, hands loose in his lap, in a room that should have been empty and rotting and was instead swept clean, with a fire laid in the stove and a bunk made up with grey wool blankets, folded down. Folded down, JT thought, like somebody was expected. And at the head of the bunk, standing in the corner where the shadows were thickest, too tall for the low ceiling so that it had to hold its head lowered — was the buck. Twelve points, maybe more, antlers brushing the beams. Utterly still. Chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. His father lifted his head. His lips parted, the way they had in the clearing, like a man on the verge of whispering a secret. And the buck turned its dark, flat eyes from his father — and looked out the window, directly at JT. Its mouth began to move. Not like an animal's mouth. Like it was trying to remember how his father's mouth had done it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The continuation is a strong piece of King-style horror writing. It preserves JT's limited, uncertain POV, introduces organic plot escalation (the Travers cabin legend delivered through natural dialogue), and builds to a genuinely unsettling payoff that extends the buck motif from Chapter One. The dialogue between Mike, the father, and JT is naturalistic and character-differentiating—Mike's teasing, the father's terse evasions. The father's transformation is foreshadowed through small physical details (trembling hands, stillness, the "wondering" voice), making his walk into the cabin feel tragically inevitable rather than arbitrary. Imagery is excellent: "a sound JT had fallen asleep to since he was six," spruces leaning "like they'd been listening," a cabin that "looked abandoned the way a held breath looks like rest." The ending image—the buck imitating human mouth movements—is a superb surreal-horror beat. Minor weaknesses: the "isolated narrator keeps everything to himself" beat is somewhat restated (the tooth metaphor and the fear-of-his-father's-look both explain the same reticence). Mike is a bit broadly drawn as the wisecracking older brother. The chapter exceeds 1000 words noticeably (closer to 1,400+), a mild instruction deviation. A few King tics feel slightly imitative rather than organic. Still, tension builds cleanly, the dread is earned, and the prose is controlled and precise. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Hell Is Other Demons** Lucifer Morningstar woke, as he had woken every morning for several thousand years, to the sound of his throne being eaten. It was not a loud sound. Hellhounds, even very large ones with three heads and a regrettable fondness for furniture, chew thoughtfully. It was a wet, metallic *scritch-scritch-scritch* from the throne room below, patient as dripping water. Lucifer lay in bed and stared at the ceiling, which was made of black basalt and old regrets. “Trevor,” he called. The chewing paused. Then, with greater enthusiasm, it resumed. Lucifer got up, put on a dressing gown the colour of a dying star, and made coffee. He made two cups out of habit, then looked at the second cup for a while. He poured it down the sink, where it hissed and accused him in Latin. He was not lonely. The Prince of Darkness, the Morning Star, the Adversary, did not get lonely. He had legions. He had dominions. He had an entire pit of the damned who screamed his name at all hours, which was almost like company, if you did not listen to the words. Lilith had moved out in March. Or possibly in 1348. Time in Hell had a union agreement and refused to work weekends. Officially, they were off again. Unofficially, Lilith had stopped by on Tuesday to return his halo polish, which he had not used since the Fall and had not asked for. On Thursday she had come to ask if he had seen her serpent. He had not. On Friday she had come over for no reason that involved violence at all, which for Lilith represented enormous personal growth. She had stayed for tea. She had criticised his curtains. He had thought about it ever since. Downstairs, Trevor had moved on to a particularly succulent part of the throne’s front left leg. One head chewed. One head watched Lucifer with moist, hopeful eyes. The third was asleep, snoring small puffs of sulphur. “No,” Lucifer told him. “Bad dog. Bad manifestation of mankind’s fear of death.” Trevor wagged his tail, which was a scorpion, and it stung a passing imp. The morning’s business began at nine. Hell, contrary to popular belief, is mostly administration. Damnation is easy. Damnation *at scale* requires forms. Mammon presented the quarterly torment figures on a spreadsheet carved into a banker. Productivity was down in the Seventh Circle. Envy was up. Lust was performing strongly but Asmodeus, as usual, was taking credit for the work of others. “We could increase eternal suffering by twelve percent,” Mammon said, “if we streamlined the screaming.” “Fine,” said Lucifer. “Whatever.” Beelzebub raised a hand, and several thousand flies. “The cafeteria is serving souls again. We’ve asked them for a vegetarian option.” “Fine.” From beneath the throne, *scritch-scritch-scritch*. Lucifer rubbed his temples. “Can nobody hear that?” The assembled Princes of Hell looked at the throne, at Trevor, and at Lucifer, in the manner of people who have worked together for eternity and know precisely which battles not to join. “It adds character, my lord,” said Mammon carefully. The throne listed, very slightly, to the left. At eleven, a delegation of demons requested permission to unionise. At noon, Lucifer signed three thousand death warrants, two interdepartmental memos, and a birthday card for Hitler, which was departmental policy and which he always signed simply *Best, L.* At one, he ate lunch alone in his office and told himself he preferred it. At two, Lilith arrived. She did not knock. Lilith had never knocked, not in Eden, not in the desert, and not in Hell. Doors tended to open for her out of good sense. “You’re letting him chew that,” she said. Lucifer looked up from a report on innovative flaying. “Hello, Lilith. Lovely to see you. How are you?” “It will go right through.” “He’s teething.” “He is nine thousand years old.” “He’s emotionally immature.” Trevor, traitorously, stopped chewing at once and rolled over. Lilith scratched his middle head behind the ears and he made a sound like a collapsing cathedral. “I only came to borrow brimstone,” she said. “I’m out.” “You live above the Lake of Fire.” “It’s not the same. Yours is finer.” She was wearing black, of course, and her hair was full of night wind although there was no wind in Hell, and she looked exactly as she had on the first bad morning of the world. Lucifer found this deeply unfair and entirely typical. He got the brimstone. He took rather longer than necessary finding it. In the kitchen, Lilith opened his fridge. “You have nothing in here except pomegranates and wrath.” “I have been busy.” “You have condiments from the Bronze Age.” “I run Hell.” “You always say that when the fridge is empty.” This was true. It had been true in several lost civilisations. They drank coffee — he made two cups again, and this time did not comment on it, and neither did she — while below them the damned wailed in four-part harmony. She told him about her garden, where the nightshade was doing well and the forbidden fruit had come in early. He told her about the throne. “You could just get a new leg,” she said. “It’s the Throne of Perdition. It was forged from the weapons of—” “It’s a chair, Luce.” “It is a symbol.” “It’s a chair with teeth marks.” *Scritch-scritch-scritch.* Trevor had resumed, quietly, as if hoping not to be noticed, which is difficult when you weigh as much as a siege engine. Lilith looked at Lucifer over her cup. “You look tired.” “I am the Prince of Darkness.” “You always say that when you haven’t slept.” There was a pause, of the sort that had once caused plagues. “Why did you really come?” he asked. “To borrow brimstone.” “You could send an imp.” “I like to stretch my legs.” She glanced away, toward the window, where a soul was being chased across the Styx by something with too many wings. “And it has been quiet in my place. The silence gets… loud.” Lucifer nodded, as if this were a normal administrative matter. She left before dinner, because leaving before dinner meant this was not a reconciliation, merely a visit, and both of them could continue to preserve the fiction with dignity. At the door she paused. “I might come tomorrow,” she said. “You probably have some of my post. Damned souls. They always deliver them to the wrong abyss.” “I probably do,” he agreed, though he did not. After she had gone, the palace was very large and very empty and full of tasteful obsidian. Trevor chewed. The throne sank another inch. Lucifer sat on it anyway, lopsided, King of Hell, Lord of the Flies, Keeper of the Pit, and ate pomegranates over the sink for dinner so he would not have to wash a plate. Before bed, he set out two cups by the coffee pot. Just in case one was needed. Just for efficiency. From below: *scritch-scritch—CRACK.* The front left leg gave way with enormous finality. There was a crash, a yelp, and then a pleased, guilty silence. Lucifer sighed, in the darkness, and almost smiled. He would have it fixed in the morning. Or possibly not.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-executed piece of comic fantasy that understands its assignment precisely. The story merges the domestic and the infernal with genuine skill: the hellhound eating the throne, the unionized demons, the birthday card for Hitler signed "Best, L." — these are exactly the kind of understated absurdist touches the prompt requested, and they land more often than not. The Lilith-Lucifer dynamic is the heart of the piece, and it's handled with restraint. Their dialogue is the strongest element: "It's a chair, Luce." / "It is a symbol." / "It's a chair with teeth marks." This is sharp, economical, character-revealing banter that does the work of showing rather than telling. The brimstone pretext, the empty fridge, the two coffee cups — these are well-chosen domestic details that ground the cosmic in the relatable. The "off again" stage is preserved with both parties' dignity intact, and the ending (two cups set out "just for efficiency") is a satisfying, understated close that doesn't force a reconciliation the premise didn't earn. The prose is clean and rhythmic, with a dry Gaiman-esque wit throughout. Occasional lines are genuinely excellent ("a dressing gown the colour of a dying star," "Time in Hell had a union agreement and refused to work weekends"). A few jokes are slightly over-egged — the "he was not lonely" paragraph spells out its irony a touch too explicitly, and the Hitler card risks tonal wobble without quite toppling. The Trevor material occasionally threatens to overstay its welcome, though the final throne-collapse beat justifies the setup. Weaknesses are minor: some mid-section business (Mammon, Beelzebub) is functional rather than inspired; the piece occasionally tells us its own jokes ("which for Lilith represented enormous personal growth" is a good line but the narrator underlines it). The emotional complexity is real but kept deliberately light — this is a comedy first, and it doesn't push into deeper feeling, which is a legitimate choice but caps its ceiling. Overall: a polished, funny, tonally consistent piece that fulfills the brief with notable craft. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 85.0
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
I woke before the trumpets, as I always did, to the smell of boiled barley and old sweat soaked into the straw beneath me. The cell was still dark, and through the barred slit above my head I could hear Rome beginning to stir beyond the walls of the ludus — cart wheels grinding on stone, a baker shouting at his boy, pigeons bursting from the tiles. Somewhere down the corridor, a man coughed, another prayed, and iron rang softly as the guards made their rounds. My name, the one they shouted in the Flavian Amphitheatre, was Verus. The name my mother gave me was Bran, and she gave it to me in a village of timber and peat smoke far north of here, where the rain tasted of iron and no one had heard Latin except from tax men and soldiers. I had not heard it spoken kindly in seven years. I sat up and pressed my thumb to the little wooden Hercules bound on a cord around my neck. My grandfather had carved him, lion skin over one shoulder, club resting easy, not raised. I liked that. Hercules had done his labors and been allowed, at last, to rest, and if any god understood a man who was owned and set to impossible tasks for the amusement of his betters, it was him. I whispered his name, not as a prayer for victory, for there was no fighting that day, but as one thanks a fellow laborer at dawn. Breakfast was barley porridge again, thick enough to stand a spoon in, with beans, a thumb of hard cheese, and water that smelled faintly of the lead pipes. We ate in the yard while the light turned the dust gold. Cassius, who had been a fisherman near Ostia before debt took him, tore his bread into careful pieces and told me, for the third time that week, exactly how he would cook mullet when he was free. Felix laughed through his broken nose and said freedom tasted better with sauce. We all laughed, because the alternative made eating difficult. The doctor came after, a Greek named Theon who smelled of vinegar and mint and treated us as valuable horses, which, to the lanista, we were. He pressed his thumbs into the scar along my ribs, asked after my sleep, and frowned at the swelling in my left knee. “You favor it,” he said. “I favor being alive,” I told him, and he snorted and rubbed in oil that burned pleasantly and left my skin shining. Above us, laundry snapped on a roof, and a woman sang while she beat a tunic, the rhythm keeping time with my pulse. Our lanista, Quintus Aurelius Rufus, arrived midmorning with a tablet under his arm and the pleased expression of a man who had smelled money on the wind. He told us the Emperor Trajan would give games on his return from the east, greater than those for Dacia, with beasts from Egypt and prisoners whose names none of us could pronounce. A murmur went through the yard, part fear, part hope, for a good showing before the Emperor could mean coins, a wooden sword, and a life no longer measured in other men’s entertainment. Rufus looked at me a moment longer than the others, and I understood that some bargain had already been made with my body in a room I would never enter. That afternoon Rufus sent me with two guards to carry a message to a fuller near the Subura, a trust that was less kindness than advertisement, for a known face draws custom and reminds debtors what collateral looks like. The street hit me like a opened oven — hot stone, frying oil, urine from the pots outside shops, crushed herbs, horse dung, and the sweet rot of garum. Porters shouldered past with amphorae knocking at their hips, children darted after a hoop, and a senator’s litter forced us all to the wall, its curtains twitching, its bearers sweating in perfect silence. At a crossroads shrine, old women left cakes for the Lares, and a scribe read a posted edict aloud to men who could not read it themselves, about grain, about taxes, about another triumph being prepared. Someone muttered that triumphs were fine for those who ate from them, and the guards pretended not to hear. Near the fuller’s shop, where steam billowed and the air stung my eyes with ash and piss used for cleaning wool, a boy no older than ten stared at the scar on my arm and whispered my arena name to his friend as if I were already a statue. His mother pulled him close, not from fear of me, I thought, but from fear that he would admire me. That was Rome in a single gesture: it fed us to the crowd for love, then crossed the street to keep its sons clean. When we returned, a letter waited that I could not read, from a trader who claimed my sister still lived beyond the frontier and would sell news of her for more silver than I would earn in a year of surviving. Theon read it twice, his face giving me nothing, and I held the wax tablet as if weight alone could tell me whether it was hope or a trap. That night we ate lentils and listened to rain begin on the tiles, washing the city’s smell down to wet dust and iron. Cassius spoke of mullet, Felix of sauce, and I touched Hercules at my throat and thought of labors no poet would sing, of a sister whose voice I was forgetting, and of Rufus smiling at money on the wind. I did not pray to be great. I prayed, if prayer it was, to be finished, and to recognize myself when I was. Outside, Rome shouted, drank, bargained, and slept under its emperor, certain of eternity, while inside our walls we counted days by scars and meals.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, well-controlled piece of historical fiction that fulfills nearly every instruction with confidence. The first-person, past-tense voice of Bran/Verus is consistent and distinctive — a mixture of weary pragmatism and lyrical observation that never breaks character. The prompt's requirements are all met: no combat scene, rich sensory detail (boiled barley, garum, fuller's ash and urine, lead-piped water), interiority, political/social texture (Trajan's games, edicts read aloud to the illiterate, the litter forcing plebeians to the wall, the mother pulling her son away from admiring the gladiator), and a clear sense of a larger story beyond this slice. Strengths: The Hercules talisman is a well-chosen, thematically resonant detail — a god who "did his labors and been allowed, at last, to rest" mirrors the gladiator's own condition without being spelled out. The street scene is the sensory centerpiece and earns its length. The observation "it fed us to the crowd for love, then crossed the street to keep its sons clean" is the piece's sharpest social insight. The unreadable letter from the trader is an effective quiet hook for the larger narrative. Supporting characters (Cassius, Felix, Theon, Rufus) are sketched economically but vividly. Weaknesses: The prose occasionally strains toward aphorism — "That was Rome in a single gesture" is the narrator explicitly telling us the significance of a moment the reader had already grasped. A few phrases ("a opened oven," "smelled money on the wind" repeated verbatim at the end) are minor blemishes; the repetition of the money-on-the-wind line reads as intentional but is slightly cute. The sister subplot is introduced and shelved within a few paragraphs, which is fine for a slice but slightly convenient as an emotional lever. Some of the social commentary, while well-integrated, covers familiar ground for the genre (bread and circuses, the owned body, the empire's certainty of eternity). The ending is well-earned but the final sentence's rhythm is a touch tidy. Dialogue is sparse but functional; Theon's exchange is characterful. Nothing meanders; the day is structured with clear purpose. Emotionally, the piece is restrained and earns its melancholy without wallowing. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
12 October 1974 Cape Wrath Lighthouse, Sutherland Dear Mam, Arrived Tuesday after a lift in the Board's lorry from Lairg, then to the Kyle of Durness and across on the ferry. Mr Sutherland, the Principal Keeper, showed me the light and my room and that was about the extent of the conversation. He is not rude. He just does not see the point in using two words when none will do. The work is cleaning, polishing, and watches through the night. The pay is better than Brown's yard paid before it shut, and there is no rent on the cottage. I will send half home on Friday. Do not worry about me eating. Mrs Sutherland left a pot of soup that would feed Partick. Your son, Tam --- 28 October 1974 14 Dowanhill Street, Partick Dear Tam, Your money came. I put ten pounds off the electric and the rest in the house book, so do not be sending more than you need to live on up there. Jean came round on Sunday with that boyfriend of hers, Colin, the one with the motorbike and no job to speak of. She says to tell you hello. The damp in the back bedroom is back again. I have told the factor twice and he has promised to look, which means he will look sometime before Christmas. Next Christmas, probably. Write when you can. I know the post is not every day. Mrs Rafferty on the stair asked after you and I said you were doing very well, which I hope is true and not just you telling me stories. Love, Mam --- 20 November 1974 Dear Mam, It gets dark before four now. My watch is ten till two, then Sutherland takes over. In the day we paint, mend fences, and carry stores up from where the boat lands below Kearvaig Bay. You can see the big sea stack out there when it is clear. Most days it is not clear. I am reading my way through Sutherland's books. Mostly about birds. He writes down every one he sees in a notebook, with the date and all. I could not tell a gannet from a gull when I came. I am improving, though not enough that I would say it out loud to him. Tell Jean that Colin had better find work before he finds himself barred from our door. Tam --- 8 December 1974 Dear Tam, I have sent a parcel with socks, a scarf, and a fruit loaf wrapped in greaseproof paper. If it arrives by February, thank the postman. Jean and Colin are engaged. He has got labouring work out at Anniesland, so your threat worked from two hundred miles away. She wants a June wedding and a three-piece suite on tick. I told her a suite does not make a marriage, but she is twenty-two and knows everything. Are you sleeping, son? Your last letter sounded cheerful in the way people are cheerful when they have rehearsed it. You do not need to do that with me. Love, Mam --- 17 January 1975 Dear Mam, The parcel came Tuesday. The loaf was fine after I cut the outside off. You asked about sleeping. I sleep in pieces. When I come off watch my head is still going round with the light, even with the curtains shut. Sutherland says you get used to it. He has been here eleven years and can go a whole meal without speaking to his wife. She goes to her sister in Durness whenever the ferry lets her. I do not blame her. I am not unhappy exactly. There is just nothing to mark one day from the next except the weather. I caught myself talking to the generator yesterday. It did not answer, which is probably for the best. Tam --- 3 February 1975 Dear Tam, Talking to a generator is not the worst thing. Your father talked to the wireless whenever Partick Thistle were playing, and that never answered him either, except once when he threw his shoe at it. But listen to me. That job was meant to keep you going after Brown's shut, not to keep you forever. If it is making you ill, you come home and we manage. We managed before. Jean says Colin can ask about labouring work. There is no shame in leaving a thing that does not suit you. Your father stayed too long at jobs that ground him down because he thought asking for help was failure. I will not watch you learn the same lesson. There. That is my speech made. Now eat properly and write back. Love, Mam --- 28 February 1975 Dear Mam, Sorry this is short. I have not been right these last weeks. Sutherland keeps a bottle in the store for "emergencies" and I have been helping myself after my watch so I can sleep. Last Tuesday I woke at half past three with him banging on my door. I had slept through the changeover. He covered for me and put my name in the log as if I had been there. He never said a word about it after. Somehow that is worse than a shouting. Do not send anything. I will write properly soon. Tam --- 19 March 1975 Dear Tam, Properly soon is not good enough. I have had your February letter three weeks and nothing since. I am not writing to scold you. God knows I have done enough of that in my life, and half the time you were only guilty of being daft. I am writing because I know the difference between you being quiet and you being stuck inside your own head. Your father had the same way of going silent, usually in February, usually with a bottle nearby. Whatever you have done, it is done. Whatever you are thinking of doing, do not do it alone in that tower. Write one line if that is all you can manage. Just write it. Mam --- 6 April 1975 Dear Mam, I am writing one line first, as ordered: I am all right. Now the rest. On Thursday night the wind took two slates off the cottage and Sutherland went up the tower at midnight because his chest was hurting and he would not say so. I found him sitting on the stair at the second landing, grey as paper, trying to get up. I got him down and onto the radio to Durness. No boat could come in that sea, and no helicopter either until morning. He kept saying, "Mind the light." So I minded it. Up and down all night, checking the lamp, winding, watching the pressure, with the whole building shaking and him lying in his kitchen telling me what to do through the open door. A fishing boat out of Kinlochbervie was close enough in to be in trouble if we went dark. I do not know if that is true or if he said it to keep me moving. It worked either way. They took him to Raigmore on Friday. Mrs Sutherland phoned the Board office and they phoned here. He is alive. It was his heart, but not the worst kind, whatever that means. I have not touched the bottle since. Not because I have turned into a saint. I keep seeing myself asleep through the changeover and him on those stairs. I was lucky, Mam. I do not want to need that kind of luck again. I have written to the Board asking to be relieved at the end of May. I do not know if I am brave or a coward for it. I know I cannot stay. Tam --- 24 April 1975 Dear Tam, You are neither brave nor a coward. You are a man who kept a light going through a bad night and has sense enough to know when a job is costing him more than it pays. That will do for me. Now I have a confession of my own. Most of the money you sent home is not spent. It is in a Post Office book in your name, in the drawer under the good tablecloth. Three hundred and eighty pounds. I took what I needed and no more. Jean knows. She said you would be furious, and maybe you will be, but I was not going to let you think you had to stay up there because your mother could not manage her rent. Mr Sutherland's wife wrote to me, by the way. A very neat hand. She said he is asking whether the bird notebook got put away dry. I said I would ask you. Eleven years and that is what the man worries about. Come home when they let you. Your room is aired. Love, Mam --- 30 May 1975 Kyle of Durness Dear Mam, I am writing this in the café waiting for the bus south. My bag is heavier than when I arrived because Mrs Sutherland made me take Sutherland's bird books. "He says you know a gannet now," she said. He is home from hospital and thinner, but well enough to complain about the hospital tea. I put his notebook on his kitchen table, dry as requested. The new keeper arrived yesterday. Young fellow from Fraserburgh, keen as anything. I showed him the light, the generator, and where the boat lands. I did not tell him the generator makes poor conversation. He will find out himself, or better, he will not need to. Colin has got me an interview on Monday with his foreman. It is only labouring to start, and the money is less, but I will take it if it is offered. I have your Post Office book money if Monday goes badly. Our money, I should say. We will argue about that on Friday. I slept nine hours last night in the lodgings here. No dreams about the light. I woke up because a lorry was reversing outside, which is an improvement. Do not make a big tea. Just make tea. I will be home for it. Tam
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece of epistolary fiction that fulfills the brief with notable discipline. The two voices are genuinely distinct: Tam's letters are clipped, practical, and understated, while Mam's are warmer, wry, and gently bossy ("Do not make a big tea. Just make tea" is a lovely closing beat). Both voices feel authentically working-class Scottish without tipping into dialect pastiche or cliché — the restraint is a real strength. The plot unfolds gradually and organically: financial worry, isolation, insomnia, the bottle, the missed watch, the crisis night with Sutherland's heart attack, and the decision to leave. The crisis is well-handled — "Mind the light" is an effective pivot, and Tam keeping the light going all night while Sutherland directs from the kitchen is concrete, dramatized, and earns the emotional weight. The mother's confession about saving the money is a genuinely good turn: it reframes the entire correspondence, revealing that her earlier insistence "we managed before" concealed a quiet financial safety net, and it gives Tam permission to leave without it feeling like failure. The resolution is satisfying and appropriately modest — no grand transformation, just a man going home to a labouring job and a cup of tea. The bird notebook detail ("He says you know a gannet now") is a well-seeded callback that gives Sutherland unexpected depth. Weaknesses are minor. The middle stretch (November–February) is somewhat low-stakes and the pacing of the crisis, while earned, arrives fairly conventionally — the drunk keeper redeemed by a heroic night is a familiar shape. The drinking thread resolves a touch neatly ("I have not touched the bottle since"). Some letters, particularly the early ones, are functional rather than vivid, and the imagery, while clean, is sparse even for the form — the sea stack and the shaking tower are the main exceptions, and they work. Occasionally the understatement tips toward the formulaic ("which is probably for the best"). Still, this is confident, controlled writing that trusts its reader. The emotional climax lands, the resolution satisfies, and the voices are the piece's greatest asset. Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Okay. Be normal. Be a person on a date, not a penetration test with appetizers. Don't scan the host stand. Don't notice that the reservation tablet is unlocked, logged in as ADMIN, and angled perfectly toward the line of people waiting for tables. Don't think about how many phone numbers and full names I could scroll through before anyone noticed. Don't think *attack surface* when I see the little paper sign taped to the register: GUEST WIFI - BellaGuest2024! I am reformed. White hat. I get paid to think like this now, between 9 and 5, with signed authorization forms and a manager named Dave who says "scope" every twelve seconds. Out of scope. She is out of scope. The restaurant is out of scope. My whole life outside work is supposed to be out of scope. Elena smiles when she sits down and I immediately forget the tablet, which is good, and notice her hands instead, which is normal, and then notice she has no screen protector and a crack in the top corner of her phone, which is not normal but is at least quiet. *Hi. You look nice. Please don't be boring. Please don't make me explain what I do and then ask if I can hack your ex's Instagram.* She doesn't. She asks about work, I give the sanitized version — "I break into companies, with permission, before criminals do it without" — and she doesn't flinch. She laughs. She says that sounds like being a professional burglar for banks. Yes. Exactly. Please keep thinking that's cool and not creepy. We're fifteen minutes in and it's... working? She likes Thai food but can't do peanuts, grew up outside Columbus — *don't file that away, that's a security question, hometown, stop it* — moved here for a library science degree, works archiving old maps. She tells me her cat is named Biscuit, after her childhood corgi, also named Biscuit, because she was six and committed to the brand. *First pet: Biscuit. Mother's — no. STOP. This is not recon. This is a woman telling you a cute story because she wants you to know her.* I want to know her. That's the terrifying part. Normally first dates are threat modeling with drinks. Is she lying about her age? Is that her real laugh? How quickly can I get to my car if this goes bad? I have an exit by the bar, another past the bathrooms that leads to the kitchen, and the kitchen door has a keypad and the busboy just punched 4-7-1-9 without shielding it. *4-7-1-9. Why did I retain that? I don't need that. Delete.* Then the waiter asks if we play anything nerdy because he saw my phone background — it's the art from Counterspell, the old Mark Poole one — and Elena's entire face changes. "You play Magic?" Oh no. Oh perfect. Commander. Of course Commander. She runs a Simic deck that she insists is "not that kind of Simic," which is exactly what that kind of Simic player says. She loves Kinnan. She hates free counterspells on principle but runs Fierce Guardianship because, and I quote, "other people can't be trusted." I run Yuriko because I like information and being hated efficiently. She says Yuriko players are red flags. I say Kinnan players shouldn't be allowed within fifty feet of a Sol Ring. She's grinning. I'm grinning. This is not small talk anymore, this is the real protocol handshake. We are arguing about whether Cyclonic Rift is a war crime. She once top-decked a Craterhoof in a library staff game and felt so guilty she bought everyone coffee. I once kept a one-land hand at a prerelease because it had Ponder and pure delusion. *Connection established. Secure channel. Do not ruin this.* She tells me about her pod back in Ohio, her brother Marcus taught her to play in 2014 — *brother's name Marcus, don't* — they still play over SpellTable on Sundays. Her mom, whose maiden name she jokes is impossible to spell, Kowalski — she actually says it, laughing, because her email is elena.kowalski-something for family stuff — *I did not ask for that. I do not want that. Why do people just broadcast the answers to 'mother's maiden name,' 'first pet,' 'city where you were born,' like they're dealing out free password resets?* Because they're not thinking like me. Because normal people experience conversation as conversation, not as an intake form for identity theft. Lucky them. I am doing so well. I order without commenting that our server wrote another table's credit card number — no, he didn't, relax, it's a loyalty number, breathe — I don't mention the POS system is running something ancient enough to have grandchildren. I listen. I ask about maps. She asks if I ever miss the other side. Yes. No. I miss how simple it was at seventeen, before I understood consequences were not just a loading screen. I got caught boosting accounts and doing stupid, selfish stuff for people who would have sold me for a pizza. I got lucky: a mentor, a diversion program, a company willing to hire the cautionary tale. Now I write reports. "Critical vulnerability: humans trust other humans." Case in point. Her phone buzzes on the table. Face down, then she flips it, and without thinking, in full view, at table height, she draws her unlock pattern. Top-left. Across. Down. Bottom corner. An L. Four dots. The most common pattern on earth. The pattern a child would guess. The pattern I have demonstrated in corporate trainings while a room full of executives goes very quiet and pretends to check their own phones. My mouth, traitor, opens before my brain can deploy any social patch. "Please tell me that's not your real pattern." Silence. The candle is suddenly very loud. She stares. "Were you watching me unlock my phone?" *Abort. Rollback. Restore from backup where I was charming and arguing about Craterhoof.* "I wasn't — I mean, I didn't try to, it was just there, and it's — that's literally the first one anyone tries. Like, anyone who found your phone could—" "So you memorized it." "I didn't memorize it, it's an L, there's nothing to memorize, that's the point." Great. Excellent. Vulnerability disclosed. Severity: critical. Exploit: me. Her shoulders go up. The secure channel is closing. She turns the phone face down again, slower this time, deliberate, and I can see her recalculating me: professional burglar for banks, right. How many other things have I catalogued tonight? Her hometown. Biscuit. Kowalski. Marcus. 4-7-1-9 on a door that isn't mine. She doesn't know I have those filed away, but she can probably see, now, that I file things. "Do you do that with everyone?" she asks. "No." Lie. "I try not to." Truth. "It's my job to notice. It's... it's how my brain got wired. Someone leaves a door open, I see the open door before I see the house." "And you have to comment on the door? On a date?" "No. I absolutely did not have to do that." At least I don't say *but your banking app*. At least I don't say *and you just told me every recovery answer except your birthday, which is on your Instagram because your friends posted a photo on March 3rd with balloons shaped like a 2 and a 9 last year* — I didn't look her up. Much. A normal amount. A creepy amount by normal standards. *Do not confess to pre-date OSINT. That is not the salvage operation here.* Salvage. What would a human do? Apologize without making it a lecture. Don't touch her phone. Don't offer to "fix" her like she's a misconfigured server. People are not systems. People are not systems. People have feelings and also, incidentally, terrible patterns. "I'm sorry," I say out loud. "That was a work reflex and it was rude. You were showing me trust just sitting here, and I turned it into a security audit. I don't want to audit you. I was having a really good time arguing about whether you're a war criminal for running Rift." A tiny pause. "I overloaded the Rift," she says, but it's cooler now. Testing. "You always overload the Rift. That's why it's a war crime." She doesn't laugh, exactly, but her mouth twitches. Her hand is still covering her phone. I put my own phone on the table, face up, and push it an inch toward her. Mine has a stupidly long passphrase. It also has, on the lock screen, a photo of my terrible prerelease deck from 2019 that I keep to humble myself. "For the record," I say, "my weakness is keeping a one-land hand because I believe in myself too much. And telling women their security sucks before dessert. Both have cost me games." That gets a real breath out. Not forgiveness. An opening. A port left intentionally — no. A door she might choose to open. She says, "If I change it, you're not watching." "Deal. I'll study the menu like it owes me money." She picks up the phone, turns away — actually turns in her chair, shoulder blocking me, smart, instinctive, see, humans learn — and changes it. I stare very hard at the dessert list. Tiramisu. I do not need to know what she changed it to. I do not want to know. I want to know if she'll still play a game with me sometime. I want to know if noticing everything means I can never just... be in a room. When she turns back, she says, "It's not an L anymore." "Good." "I'm not telling you what it is." "I would be genuinely upset if you did." She looks at me for a long moment, deciding if I'm a red flag with a Yuriko deck or just a guy whose brain runs background scans he never asked for. Then she says, "It's a lightning bolt. For my deck." *Don't guess the dot order. Don't you dare visualize it.* "Very on brand for a Simic player pretending she's not the problem." "I am not the problem. I am the ramp." And just like that, we're not fixed, but we're back in the game. At reduced life total. With blockers up. I can work with that.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of constrained-voice fiction that executes the prompt with confidence and wit. The internal monologue is nearly continuous, as requested, and the hacker's compulsive pattern-noticing is rendered through concrete, specific detail rather than abstract assertion: the unlocked host-stand tablet, the keypad code "4-7-1-9," the loyalty number misread as a credit card number. The show-don't-show discipline is impressive — the protagonist's reformation is dramatized through micro-suppressions ("Delete," "STOP") rather than backstory dumps, and the backstory that does appear (caught at seventeen, mentor, diversion program) is economical and earns the character's self-awareness. The MTG material is genuinely well-done: Yuriko vs. Kinnan, Fierce Guardianship hypocrisy, Cyclonic Rift as war crime. These aren't generic nerd signifiers; they're used structurally, as the shared language through which the couple reconnects after the breach. The phone-pattern incident lands with proper timing — the piece lets the silence sit ("The candle is suddenly very loud") and gives Elena a believable, non-cartoonish reaction: recalculating, testing, setting boundaries ("If I change it, you're not watching"). Weaknesses: the ending is a touch tidy. Elena's recovery arc — from "were you watching me unlock my phone?" to playful banter and a lightning-bolt pattern — happens fast, and the final beat ("At reduced life total. With blockers up.") is clever but slightly neat, a writer's ending rather than a lived one. The salvage is at least seeded by the earlier rapport and by the protagonist's genuine apology, so it doesn't feel fully unearned, but the forgiveness arrives a beat or two sooner than psychological realism would allow. There are also a few moments where the voice's cleverness crowds the emotion — the piece is so consistently quippy that quieter registers get less room, and the OSINT confession ("I didn't look her up. Much.") is introduced and then dropped rather than explored, which is a missed opportunity for real emotional complexity. Minor factual slip ("Mark Poole" for Mark Poole's Counterspell art is actually correct; "Cyclonic Rift" is misrendered once as "Cyclonic Rift" — trivial). The prose is clean, rhythmic, and controlled; occasionally aphoristic to a fault ("People are not systems. People are not systems.") but never purple. Coherence, adherence, and engagement are all high. The piece's main limitation is a certain sameness of register — relentless wit as armor, with the vulnerability mostly implied — and an ending slightly more resolved than the situation warrants.
