+ First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 87.8
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Four minutes. She said four, and it's been six since the last text — *almost there, sorry!!* — with two exclamation points, which could mean she's cheerful, or it could mean she's overcompensating because she feels guilty about what she's about to do. Don't. Don't start. She is six minutes late to a coffee shop, people are six minutes late, it is not a referendum on my worth, I know that, I literally said that out loud in therapy on Thursday. And yet if she walks in now I already have the face ready, the slightly hurt, slightly distant face, so she'll ask what's wrong and I'll say *nothing, I'm fine,* and then she'll know I'm not fine and she'll have to work to get it out of me, which is unfair, I know it's unfair, but also — if I don't do that, if I'm just normal and bright, she might think it's okay to keep pulling away like this. Because she has been. That's not invented. Tuesday she cancelled, Thursday she took five hours to answer a perfectly normal message, yesterday she said *we'll see* about Sunday, which is code, everyone knows *we'll see* is code for *I don't want to but I don't want to be the bad guy yet.* In my head she's already said it properly. We're sitting right here and she stirs her coffee too long and says, *I think you're reading a lot into things that aren't there,* which is her being kind about saying I'm unstable. And I say, *I'm not reading into the distance, Maya, you created it.* And she says, *This is exactly what I mean, everything becomes an accusation.* And I say — I have three versions of what I say. In one I'm calm and devastating: *Then you don't have to deal with it anymore.* In one I cry, which I hate, I hate that version most because she softens then and it works and I feel sick for wanting it to work. In the third I laugh and say *God, forget it, I'm being crazy,* and she laughs with relief and I carry the whole rotten thing home alone. In the hallway before I left I caught myself in the mirror — shoulders up around my ears, jaw clenched, one hand picking at the other until the skin was red — and I looked so braced, like someone heading into an exam they'd already failed, that I had to turn away before I started rehearsing to my own reflection. She isn't even here and I'm already resentful. That's the protective part, I can feel myself doing it: building the resentment up front so if she does reject me it will land on something hard. *Fine. She was always flaky. She only slept with me because it was convenient after Jonah, she never actually —* No. Stop. She held my face the morning after and said she’d wanted to do that for a year. She said it first. But people say things in bed. People say things when they're lonely and the light is good. People revise. By the time she gets here I've already mourned us twice and forgiven her once for something she hasn't done, and I'm exhausted, and none of it has happened. The door chimes and it's her, hair damp from the rain I didn't notice starting, my umbrella still by my door because I was too busy catastrophizing to check the weather. She sees me and her whole face — God, it does something immediate to my chest, that loosening, that stupid desperate flood — she smiles like she's genuinely pleased, not performing pleased, and she comes straight over and hugs me before she even takes her coat off, a long hug, her cold cheek against mine, and she says, “I missed you, I'm sorry I'm late, the bus just sat there.” Missed you. She said missed you. Hold onto that, that's real, her arms are real, she's squeezing tighter, not the quick pat-pat hug you give someone you're managing. Or it's guilt. Guilt makes people affectionate. Guilt makes people hug longer because they know. She sits and reaches across the table without thinking and takes my hand, thumb moving over my knuckles, and asks how the presentation went, the one I told her I was dreading, she remembered the day, she remembered the manager's name. “Did Alan finally shut up and let you finish?” And I laugh, actually laugh, and for maybe twenty seconds my brain is quiet and I'm just here, loved, chosen, remembered in detail, which is the exact thing I’ve been starving for all week, I could cry from how much I needed her to remember Alan’s name. So why am I already checking the memory for cracks? She asked, yes, but did she ask because she cares or because she knows that's what a good — whatever we are — does? Friends, lovers, the word we haven't used. See, that's it, we haven't used a word, which gives her an exit, which she probably wants, which is why she's holding my hand now, to soften — no. I know I'm spiraling. I can name it. Splitting, catastrophizing, mind-reading, Dr. Patel would have a worksheet. Naming it doesn't stop it though. It's like watching myself from the corner of the ceiling while the other me, the louder me, keeps talking over the naming. She's telling me about work, about why she's been buried, her manager dumped the Henderson account on her, she's been getting home at nine and falling asleep with her laptop open, she shows me a photo of herself asleep on her couch with spreadsheets on her chest that her roommate took. Evidence. She is offering evidence without knowing she's on trial. “I’ve been a ghost, I know,” she says. “It’s not — I kept meaning to text properly and then I'd wake up at 2 a.m. like, shit.” Ghost. She said it before I could accuse her of it, which should end this. She knows. She's sorry. She's here in the rain with damp hair holding my hand. Or she's constructing the excuse carefully because she's had three days to construct it. Or — and this is the thought that hooks deepest — she's telling the truth *and* she's relieved by the distance, both, she hasn't noticed she prefers having a reason not to see me, and when work calms down she'll have to invent another reason, and then she'll realize. She orders me the almond croissant I like without asking. She says to the barista, “He pretends he doesn't want one and then eats half of mine, so.” And she grins at me, private, teasing, the grin from her kitchen at midnight two weeks ago, and the warmth of being known like that is so intense it almost hurts, I want to live inside that sentence, *he pretends he doesn't want one.* And immediately: she does that with everyone. She's observant. It's not special. I'm one of a rotation of people whose croissant habits she knows. Except she isn't looking at her phone. That's important, count it. Phone face-down, forty minutes now, she keeps refilling my water, she asks if Sunday still works and when I hesitate — because I am testing, I know I'm testing, I hate that I know and still do it — I say “I thought you weren't sure,” and she frowns, genuinely confused, and says, “I said we'll see because my mum might visit? She decided, she's not. So Sunday? Please? I want to cook that thing I kept talking about.” Please. She said please. She wants Sunday. In my head the other Maya, the rehearsal Maya, sighs at exactly this point and says, *You're exhausting, you know that? I can't reassure you every five minutes.* And real Maya is asking if I want to split the second croissant and wiping a flake off my chin with her thumb, unselfconscious, intimate, and I am having an argument with a woman who does not exist while the real one is touching my face. I recognize that. I do. I can see the pattern so clearly for a second that I want to tell her, *Sorry, I'm doing the thing where I convict you in advance,* and maybe she’d understand, she's understood before, that night I panicked and she stayed on the phone and said *I'm not going anywhere, say it back to me.* But if I tell her every time, won't that become the reason? Won't the reassurance wear out? Isn't there a finite amount, and haven't I already used — she used the phrase *not going anywhere* and people only say that until they go. She laughs at something I say, a real laugh, head back, and reaches for my hand again under the table like she just wants contact, and my whole body believes her and my brain, traitor, beloved, broken alarm, whispers: *enjoy it, then, but don't get used to it, remember how this felt so you can prove later that it changed.* I squeeze her hand back. I choose Sunday. I choose to stay in the chair and eat the croissant and let her tell me about Henderson, and underneath the choosing the rehearsal is already starting again for Sunday, quieter now, but starting — what I'll wear, what she'll mean if she's tired, what I'll say if she cancels, how I won't be the one to text first on Monday, how I definitely, definitely will.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece of interiority-driven fiction that fulfills nearly every instruction in the prompt with precision and genuine craft. The narrative stays almost entirely in internal monologue as requested, cycling convincingly between anticipated rejection, rehearsed confrontation (the three versions of the imagined argument are a standout structural touch), and preemptive resentment ("building the resentment up front so if she does reject me it will land on something hard"). The actual events are handled exactly as specified: Maya arrives warm, apologetic, affectionate — the missed-you hug, remembering Alan's name, the almond croissant, the "please" about Sunday — and each gesture is received with desperate, flooding relief, then immediately interrogated and corroded ("Or it's guilt. Guilt makes people affectionate"). The cognitive dissonance is rendered with rare fidelity: the narrator names his patterns (splitting, catastrophizing, mind-reading, Dr. Patel's worksheet) and explicitly notes that naming doesn't stop them — "watching myself from the corner of the ceiling while the other me, the louder me, keeps talking over the naming." This is the requested selective self-awareness, executed without therapy-speak overload. The prose is controlled and specific: the umbrella left by the door because he was "too busy catastrophizing to check the weather," the photo of Maya asleep with spreadsheets on her chest offered as "evidence without knowing she's on trial," the "rehearsal Maya" arguing with him while the real one wipes a flake off his chin. The ending is honest rather than redemptive — he chooses Sunday, but the rehearsal for Sunday is already beginning — which avoids both incongruent positivity and unearned transformation. Minor criticisms: the "traitor, beloved, broken alarm" triad flirts with overwroughtness; the pattern of warm-event-followed-by-skeptical-rebuttal is repeated enough times that the rhythm becomes slightly predictable in the middle third; and a few lines ("I could cry from how much I needed her to remember Alan's name") edge toward telling. The dialogue that exists (real Maya's) is natural and characterful, though sparse by design. These are small deductions against an otherwise exceptional piece. + Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 76.3
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Debt The rain had stopped an hour before midnight, but water still dripped from the abandoned temple's broken roof and pooled between the courtyard stones. The courtyard was twenty paces square. A cracked altar stood against its north wall, a collapsed gate opened to the south, and two rows of leaning pillars marked the east and west edges. Between the pillars, supporters from both schools formed a tight, shouting ring, waving cash, invoking ancestors, and wagering pride as eagerly as money. Kenji Sato stood on the north side, facing south, his back three paces from the altar. Barefoot on the wet stone, he wore a dark training jacket bound at the waist and a red-and-black armband knotted above his right elbow. He was twenty-three, tall through the shoulders, his hair tied back, his jaw set with inherited certainty. Jigen-ryū had been carried by samurai retainers in his family for generations, and Kenji spoke of it as others spoke of blood itself: pure, decisive, untouchable. Six paces south of him, facing north, Liu Wei rolled his neck once and settled his weight low. He was shorter, leaner, built through the hips and back, with callused knuckles and a red-and-black armband above his left elbow. Where Kenji had learned in a polished hall, Liu had learned Piguaquan in market alleys and escort yards, from men who guarded caravans and settled disputes where no rules survived contact. He looked at Kenji's straight spine and smiled as if at a beautiful, expensive vase. No master had sanctioned this. Both schools had forbidden it after the last duel, thirty years earlier, left two men crippled and a feud burning through another generation. That was why they had come without blades, at midnight, with only their senior students as witnesses. Bare hands, first man unable to rise. The debt, they agreed, would be paid in public humiliation. An old coin spun into the air between them. It struck stone, rang, and settled. Kenji moved first, exactly as everyone knew he would. He exploded south in a straight line, left foot driving, right foot crashing down ahead of it. His right arm rose high beside his ear and fell in a single overhead chop toward Liu's left collarbone, the edge of his hand standing in for the sword he had trained with since childhood. The strike cut the air fast enough to hiss. Liu did not meet it. As Kenji's front foot landed two paces from him, Liu pivoted on his left heel toward his own right — east — and dropped his head under the chop. Kenji's hand sliced past Liu's shoulder and down through empty space. His momentum carried him one full step south of where Liu had stood, chest open, right arm extended low. Liu completed his pivot facing west, already inside Kenji's left flank. His right arm swung wide from behind his hip, loose at the shoulder, then snapped rigid at the last instant as the back of his forearm whipped across Kenji's ribs. The crack echoed off the pillars. Kenji grunted, twisted north to face him, and cut back with a horizontal backhand aimed at Liu's temple. Liu ducked, felt the hand graze his hair, and retreated two quick steps east, restoring three paces between them. They circled now, Kenji turning clockwise to keep Liu centered, Liu sliding sideways along the eastern pillars, never offering a straight target. Liu's hands rose and fell in long circles, palms open, arms cracking like wet rope whenever he tested the distance with a chopping feint. Kenji ignored the feints. He advanced in short, violent bursts, each step narrowing Liu's room, forcing him gradually from the east side toward the center, then west. At the courtyard's midpoint, Kenji saw Liu's right heel touch a puddle and charged. He came in from Liu's front-left, right hand descending diagonally toward the neck. Liu slipped west and south, avoiding the worst of it, but Kenji had anticipated the retreat this time. Instead of overcommitting, Kenji planted his left foot, pivoted south, and cut off Liu's path with a second, shorter chop to the chest. The heel of his hand struck sternum and drove Liu backward the remaining two paces into the west pillar. Stone dust burst from the cracked column. Pinned with his shoulders against the pillar and Kenji directly in front of him, Liu had nowhere left to circle. Kenji pressed his left forearm across Liu's upper chest, raised his right hand beside his head, and prepared the finishing chop. The Jigen-ryū supporters roared from behind Kenji, already spending their winnings. Liu dropped instead of pulling away. His knees bent, hips sinking straight down along the pillar, and Kenji's forearm slid from his chest to his shoulder. The chop fell, striking stone where Liu's neck had been and numbing Kenji's hand to the wrist. In the same descent, Liu turned his left side toward the pillar, slipped south past Kenji's planted left leg, and whipped his right elbow backward into Kenji's floating ribs. Kenji folded around the blow. Liu continued his turn, came up behind Kenji's left shoulder, and chopped down with his left palm across the back of Kenji's right arm, driving it farther across his body. Now their positions had reversed. Kenji faced west, chest nearly touching the pillar. Liu stood southeast of him, at his back-left, with open courtyard behind him. Liu struck twice before Kenji could turn: a long right chop across the shoulder blades, then a left palm that slapped against Kenji's ear and snapped his head sideways. Kenji spun east with a wild horizontal cut. Liu leaned back at the waist, let it pass before his throat, then stepped southeast, pulling Kenji's pursuit back toward the center. They met again on the central stones, both breathing hard. Kenji's right hand was red from the pillar. Liu's chest bore a rising bruise where he had been driven back. Kenji attacked in combination for the first time — overhead chop, reverse horizontal cut, then a stepping thrust with the edge of his left hand. Liu gave ground northward step by step, arms wheeling to parry outward rather than block directly. Each contact stung, but each parry turned Kenji slightly off line, until Liu's back foot touched the first step of the northern altar. Kenji saw the trap closing. He lunged north, closing the final pace, and his third strike landed clean: the left hand that Liu redirected still drove through, its heel catching Liu above the right eye. Blood opened immediately and sheeted down one side of Liu's face. Liu staggered east along the altar step. Kenji followed, chin high, certain the next blow would end it. That certainty slowed him by half a breath. Instead of retreating farther east, Liu planted his right foot, reversed direction, and drove west directly across Kenji's front. His left arm swept up in a broad circle, clearing Kenji's guard outward to Kenji's right. His right arm followed in the opposite arc, whipping down across Kenji's left forearm and continuing into a chop against the side of his neck. Kenji's head jerked, but his feet kept carrying him east from his lunge. For an instant, his weight stood entirely on his front leg. Liu seized it. He stepped behind that leg with his own left foot, hooked the ankle, and chopped again — not harder, but downward, through Kenji's shoulder line, while his hip turned sharply. Kenji's support vanished. He fell southeast, away from the altar, and struck the courtyard stones on his right hip and shoulder. He rolled once with the momentum, came up on one knee at the center, and immediately launched himself north again in fury, refusing to acknowledge what everyone had seen. His right foot skidded in the puddle at the center. The slip was small — a hand's breadth — but it broke his charge at its root. His knee buckled inward, his overhead chop started late, and Liu was already moving. Liu stepped west off the line, let the descending hand pass his right shoulder, then pivoted behind Kenji as the taller man stumbled south. Liu's left palm struck between his shoulder blades, adding Liu's turning weight to Kenji's own broken momentum. Kenji went down face-first two paces from the southern gate, palms slapping stone, forehead stopping a finger's width from the broken step. Liu followed him down without hesitation. He dropped his right knee beside Kenji's ribs, trapped Kenji's right wrist against the wet courtyard with his left hand, and raised his right arm high. The arm circled once, gathering the whole rotation of his back and waist, then stopped with the edge of his hand resting against the side of Kenji's neck. Not striking. Showing. Silence swallowed the temple. Kenji tried to rise. Liu shifted his knee an inch closer, kept the wrist pinned, and pressed the hand-edge only slightly harder. Kenji understood the geometry as clearly as everyone watching: his arm was trapped, his neck exposed, his base gone. After three seconds, he flattened his free palm against the stone in surrender. Liu stood, blood still running from his brow, and offered no hand. Kenji rose alone, face burning, his red-and-black armband dark with rain and dust. Around them, money changed hands in stunned quiet. The debt had not ended the feud — nothing so old ended in one night — but in the ruins, before both schools, the commoner's son had made the samurai's heir kneel in the mud, and had chosen to let him stand again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a disciplined, well-constructed fight narrative that takes the prompt's central demand—physical coherence and spatial legibility—seriously and largely delivers. The opening establishes the arena with unusual precision: a twenty-pace courtyard, altar north, gate south, pillars east and west, fighters placed with distances and facing directions noted. This scaffolding pays off throughout, as nearly every exchange can be tracked: Kenji's overhead chop missing when Liu pivots east, the pin against the west pillar, the reversal of positions, the trap at the altar steps, and the final slip in the central puddle (a puddle seeded in the first paragraph and again mid-fight—good Chekhovian economy). The choreography is the piece's greatest strength. Each beat follows logically from the last: momentum is conserved, weight shifts are explained, and the fighters' styles are consistently characterized—Kenji's linear, explosive, sword-derived Jigen-ryū offense versus Liu's circular, evasive, whipping Piguaquan counters. The styles aren't just labeled; they shape the tactics (Kenji cutting off retreat angles, Liu refusing straight lines). The finish—Liu's reversal off the altar, the ankle hook, the puddle slip, and the mercy choke-hold with the shown-but-not-struck hand-edge—is a satisfying, earned climax that resolves character as well as combat. Weaknesses: the prose is functional rather than beautiful, occasionally slipping into mechanical stage-direction ("Now their positions had reversed") that reads like choreography notes rather than fiction. The characters are archetypes more than people—Kenji's "inherited certainty" and Liu's class resentment are stated rather than dramatized, and there's no interiority beyond posture and gesture. The class-conflict theme is handled competently but without surprise; the ending sentence ("the commoner's son had made the samurai's heir kneel in the mud") spells out what the fight already showed. Dialogue is essentially absent (a coin toss and silence), so that criterion is largely moot. The crowd of supporters is generic—waving cash, roaring—doing thematic work without texture. Emotional complexity is thin: pride, fury, and mercy are present but rendered at a single, somewhat flat register. Still, the piece does what most fight scenes fail to do: the reader can genuinely visualize it. The mercy ending is earned by Liu's established pragmatism rather than sentimentality, and the refusal of a neat reconciliation ("nothing so old ended in one night") avoids incongruent positivity. It's a very good genre execution with limited literary ambition. + Physical-spatial: Breaking Formation — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The speakers in each corner of Studio B blast the same track a hair too loud, so loud my teeth feel the kick drum before my ears do. It is 6:04 a.m. in Seoul, and I am standing in the back row, third from the left, where scholarship kids learn to disappear. My sneakers are scuffed, my Korean is broken, and my reflection in the floor-to-ceiling mirror looks like it took the wrong subway and never got off. Back home in the South Bronx, nobody counted your angles. You earned space by taking it. Here, space is assigned. Tape decides. Blue tape crosses mark our positions on the pale wood: front diamond, two staggered lines behind, no one drifting an inch without permission. I am number fourteen, left wing of the second line, shoulder aligned behind Jiho's right shoulder, close enough to see sweat darken his collar. Instructor Kang stands center front, facing the mirror, black cap low, whistle unused because his voice does the cutting. They call him The Surgeon. He breaks idols down to bone, then rebuilds them identical and shining. Again, he says, in English for me. Five, six, seven, eight. The bass hits us together. Hard. On one, we step right foot diagonally forward, knee locked, toe pointed, weight punching down through the heel while our left arm snaps across the chest, palm flat, elbow at exactly ninety degrees. On two, the left foot slides to meet it, no bounce, torso isolated, chin down, eyes up into the mirror. On three and four, we ripple only our shoulders, right left right, while our feet stay planted like screws. Everyone else is a machine with matching parts. I am late by a breath. Not much, just enough. My body wants to ride behind the beat, to let the snare pull my hips into a groove, to freestyle the transition with a glide and a chest pop that melts into the next count. Kang stops the music with one raised finger. Silence lands harder than sound. Fourteen, he says. Your elbow is dreaming. Again. We reset to formation, feet returning to tape, breath steaming in the cold studio air that smells like disinfectant and expensive shoes I cannot afford to ruin. My roommate paid more for his practice sneakers than my mother paid for rent the month I auditioned by video in our kitchen. I remember her holding the phone steady while I krumped around the table, careful not to kick the rice cooker. Here, my power reads as mess. Five, six, seven, eight. This time I nail the step, the snap, the shoulder isolation, but on five my street training betrays me. The choreography demands a sharp head turn to the right, chin level, gaze fixed on the side mirror, then a freeze. Instead, my neck rolls. It is muscle memory, a smooth cervical wave borrowed from breaking, where my head leads a floor spin and my spine follows like water. Here it looks like disobedience. My knee softens too, absorbing rhythm, turning their staccato line into something swung and human. Kang walks down the center aisle between the diamond and our line, stopping directly in front of me, close enough that I must look up without breaking chin position. You dance like the music owes you, he says quietly. Here, you owe the music. Every debt paid on count. Yes, seonsaengnim, I say, bowing fifteen degrees because thirty feels like surrender and zero gets you sent home. He studies my hands, still loose at my sides, fingers wanting to flick on the offbeat. Talent is not the problem, he says. Attitude lives in your joints. Looseness is not freedom here. It is noise. We run the chorus twelve times. The sequence travels: from back line we pivot on the left ball of foot, cross right over left, unwind into a low plié facing stage left, then drive four marching steps forward through the gaps in the front diamond. If my timing is early, I will collide with Minseo; if late, I leave a hole the camera will find like a missing tooth. On the ninth run, sweat makes my left foot slip half an inch inside my shoe during the pivot, my ankle wobbles, and my arms windmill once before I recover into the plié a fraction low. Nobody laughs. That is worse. These trainees have been polished since childhood, their bodies fluent in synchronization, in hitting the same angle at the same millisecond, in breathing without showing it. I learned in cyphers, in circles where you wait your turn then explode, where a b-boy freezes on one hand and the crowd decides if you lived. My style is conversation. Theirs is unison. Call and response versus one voice, perfectly tuned. During water break, I stay on my tape mark while others stretch along the barre, afraid that if I move casually I will forget where I belong. Jiho whispers, Watch my shoulder, not the mirror. It helps. On the next run I fix my eyes on the seam of his shirt, match his inhale, step when he steps, and for eight counts we move as one clean line. It feels powerful and terrifying. Powerful because the formation opens and closes around me like a lung; terrifying because I cannot hear myself inside it. If I succeed here, will my mother still recognize my dancing on television, smoothed of Bronx corners, my tutting geometric but obedient, my popping timed to a camera cut instead of a drummer's grin? Kang calls the final run. This one decides who centers the bridge tomorrow. The bridge is eight counts of exposure: advance to center, hit a chest isolation, drop, rise, turn, freeze. I could add my signature, a loose ankle roll into a Harlem shake ghosting under the isolation, invisible to judges but alive in my bones. Music roars; I breathe, plant both feet on tape, choose precision today, saving rebellion for a stage big enough to hold it whole.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a tightly controlled first-person narrative that fulfills nearly every prompt requirement with precision. The spatial tracking is exemplary: tape marks, formation geometry (front diamond, staggered lines), the narrator's position as number fourteen, the traveling sequence through the diamond—all are consistently tracked and physically coherent. The collision of street and commercial styles is rendered in authentic technical vocabulary (krump, tutting, popping, cervical wave from breaking, plié, isolation, sync versus swung timing), and the muscle-memory betrayal moment (the neck roll on count five) is a well-chosen concrete incident rather than an abstraction. The prose is lean and rhythmic, mirroring its subject—short declarative sentences land like counts ("On one... On two..."). Class anxiety and culture shock are shown through telling details: the roommate's sneakers versus mother's rent, the video audition around the rice cooker, "bowing fifteen degrees because thirty feels like surrender." Kang's dialogue is minimal but sharp ("Your elbow is dreaming"; "Attitude lives in your joints"), and the narrator's internal monologue sustains the threat of losing an authentic movement voice without stating it flatly. Weaknesses are minor. The ending's decision point—choosing precision while "saving rebellion for a stage big enough to hold it whole"—is resolved a bit too neatly and quickly for the weight of the dilemma; a slightly rushed final paragraph compresses what could be a more agonized choice. Some metaphors flirt with familiarity (mirror/subway, "missing tooth"), and the "Surgeon" instructor is a recognizable archetype, though the piece knows this and doesn't overplay him. The piece is disciplined to the point of occasional austerity—there's little narrative surprise, but the execution is strong enough that this reads as control rather than dullness. No purple prose, no meandering, no tonal breaks; the voice is consistent and confident throughout. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 87.2
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Court of the Dreaming had been a throne room that morning, a library at noon, and — because someone had filed the paperwork in triplicate — a courtroom by evening. Dream sat at the high bench, pale and still, in robes blacker than the space between stars. Before him were two lecterns, a witness box made from a child's bedframe, and, in the corner, a single, giant hourglass. It dripped shimmering sand. Occasionally, when someone was lying, a grain fell upward. "All rise," croaked Matthew the raven from the bailiff's perch. No one rose. Several litigants had no legs. One was legally a puddle. Dream closed his eyes for slightly longer than a blink. "Lucien. Read the matter." Lucien, the librarian, adjusted his spectacles and opened a book that had not existed until he needed it. "Case four thousand and twelve. *First Love v. Mora.* Dispute over territorial rights to a recurring dreamscape. Dreamer: Max Ellery, aged fourteen. Human. Alive, despite recent events." "Thank you," said Dream, in the tone of a man thanking no one. First Love took the stand first. She was rosy-cheeked and slightly bashful, with ribbons in her hair and ink on her fingers, and she kept looking at the floor as if the floor had complimented her. "State your claim," said Lucien. "It was a *field*," she said. "I made it over three months. Wildflowers. Late summer. His crush — Sophie, from chemistry, she doesn't know his surname yet, which is important — she laughs at something he hasn't quite said. They lie down. Their hands almost touch. *Almost.* That's the whole architecture. Then she leans over him, and they almost kiss, and he wakes up pleasantly confused and writes terrible poetry. It's formative." "And the defendant?" asked Dream. First Love went rosier. "She ruined it." "How?" "She got *in* the Sophie." There was a small, sympathetic murmur from the gallery, mostly from minor anxieties who had also gotten in the Sophie in other dreams. "Explain." "The leaning is mine. The mounting is — well, Sophie sits up, playfully, straddling him. That's still mine. It's daring, for fourteen. Then her face..." First Love shuddered with professional outrage. "Her face goes wrong. Longer. Hungrier. Her hair fills the sky. She sits on his chest — properly sits, with *weight* — and he can't move, and she drinks his breath out of his mouth while he stares up at her, terrified." "And?" said Dream. "And *confused*," said First Love. "He wakes up screaming and — and pleasantly confused. That's my confusion. She stole my confusion and put teeth in it." Dream looked at the defendant. Mora lounged at her lectern as if it were a windowsill she intended to haunt later. She was tall and gaunt and beautiful in the way a drowning is beautiful from very far away. She wore black, which in the Dreaming is less a colour than a commitment. "Mora," said Dream. "You have heard the claim." "I have." "You invaded a crafted dreamscape, subverted its intended emotional arc, assumed the form of the dreamer's beloved, sat upon his chest, induced paralysis, and fed upon his breath." "Yes," said Mora. "For eleven consecutive nights." "A girl's gotta eat too, you know?" The hourglass dripped. A grain fell upward. Dream stared at her. His face, which had survived the births and deaths of gods without expression, developed the faintest suggestion of a headache. "That," he said, "is your defence." "It's a good one. I'm starving out there. Nobody believes in me anymore. They have apps. They track their sleep. They say, 'Oh, it was just sleep paralysis, it was just my brain waking up before my body.' Very scientific. Very hurtful. Meanwhile *she*—" Mora jerked a thumb at First Love "—is laying out picnics in a field that smells of cut grass and hormones. Do you know how much breath a boy holds when the girl he likes climbs on top of him?" "No," said Dream. "Gallons. And then she never kisses him! Eleven months of almost! I did him a favour. At least with me something *happens.*" First Love made a noise like a valentine being torn. "Something happens? He wet the bed on Tuesday!" "From terror," Mora conceded. "Mostly." "Order," said Matthew, without conviction. Dream raised one finger. The room, including several concepts, fell silent. "Bring in the dreamer." Max Ellery was led in by two dream-wardens. He was asleep, which was legally necessary and personally inconvenient. He wore pyjamas patterned with rockets and shuffled in a translucent dream-body, eyes half-open. "Max," said Dream. "You understand you are under oath." "Is this detention?" said Max. "No." "Is Sophie here?" "No," said Dream, and then, after a pause, "not as such." Max was shown the dreamscape. Lucien turned the hourglass on its side — a procedural violation nobody challenged — and the shimmering sand spilled into the air and became, briefly, a field of wildflowers. A boy. A girl. Sunlight that remembered being warm. The girl laughed, lay down, leaned over. Her shadow lengthened. Her smile lengthened further. She settled, heavy as a secret, onto the boy's chest, and lowered her mouth to his, and drank the small silver thread of his breath while his hands twitched in the grass and could not rise. Max watched with the expression of a boy reviewing evidence against himself. "Well?" said Dream. "It was scary," said Max. "Yes." "Really scary. Like, I couldn't breathe. Like, I thought I was gonna die." "Yes." Max looked at Mora. Mora, out of ancient professional habit, looked back at him from slightly too close, although she had not moved. "Was she —" Max swallowed. "Was she still kind of...?" First Love buried her face in her hands. "Answer carefully," said Dream. "You are creating precedent." "I dunno," said Max miserably. "She had Sophie's hair. And she was looking at me like — like I was the only thing in the world. Just... hungrily. Is that bad?" "It is contested," said Dream. Lucien turned the hourglass upright. The field collapsed back into sand. Dream sat for a long time. Somewhere in his kingdom, an ocean was dreaming of being a desert, a dead king was refusing to stay buried, and the Corinthian had filed another request for unsupervised access to eyeballs. And here he was, Lord of Stories, adjudicating whether terror had improperly fondled a crush. His left eye did something it had not done since the French Revolution. It twitched. "I have reached a decision," he said. Both entities straightened. "This court finds that the dreamscape belongs to neither of you. It belongs, as all dreams ultimately do, to the dreamer." He let that noble principle settle. Then his mouth curved, almost imperceptibly, which in Dream constitutes mischief of a high and dangerous order. "However. Custody will be shared." "What?" said both of them. "The dream will proceed as First Love has crafted it. The field. The flowers. The almost-touch. The almost-kiss. First Love, you will retain authorship of the confusion." First Love beamed. "Mora, at the moment of the almost-kiss, you may enter. You may assume the beloved's shape. You may sit. You may feed." Mora beamed, with more teeth. "You may take," Dream continued, "one breath. The gasp. No more. And you will return it." Mora's smile faltered. "Return it how?" "As a sigh. Into his mouth. Gently." Dream folded his hands. "So that he wakes terrified, breathless, and pleasantly confused, and neither of you can ever fully prove which part was yours. Furthermore, you will co-author his dreams for the next year. Together. Weekly. Lucien will provide a schedule and a small office." First Love stared. "But she'll make it frightening." "Yes," said Dream. "First love is." Mora stared. "But she'll make it *tender.*" "Yes," said Dream. "So is suffocation, if done by the right person. I am told." He rose. This time, everyone who could, did. "Case dismissed," he said, and added, with the weary satisfaction of a god who has made his problem into someone else's education, "Court is adjourned. Feed responsibly." The hourglass dripped shimmering sand, and every grain, for once, fell in the right direction.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a highly accomplished piece of dark comic fantasy that executes nearly every instruction with precision. The courtroom farce is well-grounded in Sandman lore (Lucien, Matthew, the Corinthian) without becoming fan-service; the details are deployed with wit (the hourglass grain falling upward when someone lies is an excellent invention). Dream's irritation is rendered through understatement — the eye twitch "it had not done since the French Revolution," the "headache" suggestion — which suits the character perfectly. Mora's defense is given genuine pathos (obsolescence, sleep-tracking apps) which elevates her beyond caricature, and First Love's "professional outrage" is a lovely comic register. The dialogue is the strongest element: sharp, character-differentiated, and consistently funny ("No one rose. Several litigants had no legs. One was legally a puddle"). The resolution — shared custody, one breath taken and returned as a sigh — is both mischievous and thematically apt, satisfying the "tempted to mischief" instruction elegantly. Max's testimony ("Was she still kind of...?") lands the dark-comic confusion the prompt requested. Minor criticisms: the ending's aphorisms ("First love is." / "So is suffocation, if done by the right person") flirt with being too neat, and the piece occasionally leans on its own cleverness — a few jokes (the Corinthian's eyeball request) are garnish rather than function. The prose is polished but a couple of the witticisms feel writerly rather than organic. The "small office... a schedule" bureaucratic gag is a familiar register. These are small quibbles against a piece that is coherent, economical, tonally consistent, and genuinely funny while preserving darkness. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 58.0
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates, hinting at a hurried departure. Mud clings to its spokes, and fresh ruts scar the road beyond the palisade. No bells ring. No dogs bark. Smoke rises from cold chimneys and dies beneath a swollen red moon. Yennefer of Vengerberg stands in the empty square and studies the silence as another woman studies a battlefield. Her black hair moves in a wind that touches nothing else. Violet eyes narrow. The scent of lilac and gooseberries cuts through rot, iron, and old ash. Something devours this village before she arrives, and something still lingers. She lifts one gloved hand, and blue sparks crawl between her fingers. "Show yourself," she says. Laughter answers from the church roof. It rolls low and delighted across the stones. A tall figure unfolds from the shadow of the cross. A red coat spreads like spilled wine. A wide-brimmed hat shadows orange lenses, and white gloves gleam as impossibly large handguns settle at his sides. Alucard smiles with too many teeth. "A sorceress," he says. "How refreshing. The cattle only scream." Yennefer does not step back. Her chin rises. "A vampire," she replies. "How tedious. The dead rarely know when they bore the living." His smile widens. He drops from the roof. Stone cracks beneath his boots, yet he lands with a courtier's grace. He circles her, coat whispering, gaze devouring every detail. She turns with him, never offering her back, never hurrying. Power answers power in the narrow space between them. "You smell of storms and berries," he says. "And of hunger older than your beauty." "You smell of graves and arrogance," she says. "One suits you." He laughs again, and the sound strokes the nape of her neck like a cold thumb. Revulsion tightens her stomach. Fascination tightens it further. His presence presses against her wards, not breaking them, merely tasting their edges. No lesser vampire survives her first spell. This one admires the trap before he steps around it. "What do you want?" she asks. "Entertainment," he says. "A worthy opponent. Perhaps someone who ends this tedious immortality." "Then find a mirror and practice," she says. His eyes flare behind the lenses. For an instant, hunger strips the amusement from his face and reveals the abyss beneath. Yennefer sees centuries of slaughter, kings on pikes, battlefields drowning in blood. She also sees restraint, leashed by will and by some distant master's command. That restraint interests her more than the slaughter. "You serve someone," she says. His guns rise in one fluid motion. "Careful, witch." "Sorceress," she corrects. "Witches cackle over turnips. I move courts." A silver bullet tears through the air between them and strikes a corpse behind her. The corpse jerks upright with a second mouth splitting its throat. It shrieks and lunges. Yennefer spins and hurls lightning. White fire consumes the creature before Alucard's second shot echoes. Ash rains over her black dress. More shapes rise from wells, doorways, and the open church. The villagers return, wrong in every joint, with hunger wearing their faces. "Your flock?" she asks. "Insults," he says. "Weak things drink and make more weakness. They accept the night but not its nature." Contempt hardens his voice. He fires without looking, and a creature loses its head. Yennefer raises both hands. A portal tears open above the square, violet and screaming with wind. Three creatures vanish into it. Their severed limbs rain onto a distant roof. Alucard watches the portal as a starving man watches a feast. "Beautiful," he murmurs. The word sends an unwelcome heat through her. She answers by dropping the portal onto him. Space folds. His body stretches, breaks, and scatters into bats, smoke, and laughing shadow. An instant later, he stands behind her, close enough that his coat brushes her sleeve. "My turn," he whispers. She elbows backward, but her arm passes through mist. His hand closes around her wrist without quite touching skin. Cold radiates through her glove. She twists, summons fire, and forces him to release her or burn. He releases her and applauds slowly. Blackened flesh knits across his palm. Bones slide beneath skin. Regeneration fascinates her despite the horror of it. Her magic remakes her own body once, at terrible cost. His body remakes itself endlessly, carelessly, obscenely. Envy pricks her, sharp and shameful. "Does it hurt?" she asks before pride seals her mouth. His amusement softens into something almost honest. "Always," he says. "Pain reminds monsters that existence still demands payment." A creature lunges at her exposed side. Alucard catches it by the throat and crushes its spine. "Do not touch her," he tells the corpse. "She is not yours." Possession in his tone irritates her instantly. "I belong to no one," she says, and lightning crowns her hair. "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." "No," he agrees. "You are a queen pretending not to notice a throne." The compliment lands because it contains no flattery, only recognition. She refuses to let him see that. Instead, she opens her arms and calls the storm. Clouds churn beneath the blood moon. Rain falls upward from the square. Every dead thing shrieks as magic floods the stones. Alucard spreads his arms and welcomes the deluge. Lightning strikes him seven times. His coat burns. His hat rolls into the mud. His body breaks apart and reforms with each strike, laughing louder every time. Fear finally touches her, not of death, but of futility. How does anyone kill a thing that treats annihilation as applause? She changes tactics. The storm stops mid-breath. Silence becomes a blade. Yennefer steps close, invading his space as boldly as he invades hers. She presses two fingers to his chest, directly over a heart that refuses rhythm. "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame," he says. She understands then: chains bind him, and he tests their strength through her. Neither lowers their gaze first.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a tightly controlled, atmospheric encounter that fulfills the prompt's core requirements: medieval European setting, present tense, third person, shifting power dynamic, mutual repulsion and fascination, and roughly the requested length. Both characters' canonical details are woven in effectively—Alucard's red coat, hat, orange lenses, silver bullets, regeneration, contempt for weak vampires, and his Hermes quote; Yennefer's violet eyes, lilac and gooseberries, sarcasm, refusal to be possessed, and her famous line. The integration of the quotes feels mostly organic rather than pasted in. Strengths: The prose is disciplined and rhythmic, favoring short declarative sentences that create tension. The opening establishes dread economically (abandoned cart, silent bells, blood moon). The dialogue crackles—"Then find a mirror and practice" is a genuinely sharp retort, and "You are a queen pretending not to notice a throne" lands as earned recognition rather than flattery. The action beats (the portal, the storm, the corpse-villagers) escalate sensibly, and the theme of envy—Yennefer coveting his effortless regeneration against the terrible cost of her own transformation—is a smart, character-true emotional core. The ending, with both refusing to lower their gaze, honors the "neither willing to show weakness first" instruction. Weaknesses: The style is heavily mannered—staccato fragments ("Violet eyes narrow." "His smile widens.") become a tic, and the relentless parallelism occasionally tips into overwrought ("Revulsion tightens her stomach. Fascination tightens it further."). Some images strain ("the sound strokes the nape of her neck like a cold thumb"). The plot is thin: arrive, banter, fight minions, storm, stalemate—essentially a single scene with no arc beyond mutual assessment, and the ending is more a held pose than a resolution. The "he serves someone" observation is introduced and dropped. Minor logic wobble: she drops a portal "onto him" after he admires it, but the mechanics blur. The villagers-as-victims are functional set dressing rather than felt horror. Still, this is confident, controlled writing with authentic voices for both characters and several memorable exchanges. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Prison Strings The chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by, and Jolyne Cujoh counts every rattle like a second heartbeat. Green Dolphin Street Prison now holds more than Stand users, and its new west wing hums with salt lines, iron sigils, barred prayers, and devil-proof glass. Guards call the annex the Aquarium, because everything inside watches, waits, and dreams of biting through the tank. Jolyne walks the yellow line with her hair in two tight buns, her butterfly tattoo bare, and her jaw set against the Florida heat. She trusts the heat more than she trusts the new administrator who stands beside the basketball hoop with a clipboard and a gentle smile. The woman wears a crisp white shirt, a black tie, and no visible restraints, although every camera in the yard tracks her. Auburn hair falls in a braid over her shoulder, and ringed yellow eyes rise slowly, as if Jolyne already belongs in her file. “You must be Jolyne Cujoh,” the woman says, soft as a nurse. “I am Makima, from Public Safety. I oversee difficult cases.” Jolyne stops outside arm’s reach. “Funny,” she says. “Difficult cases usually get a lawyer, not a model with prison keys.” Makima smiles wider, and the expression never touches the cold center of her eyes. “Your file interests me. A false murder charge, a famous father, and a body that becomes string.” Jolyne folds her arms. “My file also says I hate questions.” Makima tilts her head, perfectly pleasant. “Then I offer answers. I know Jotaro Kujo searches for the man who frames you. I know this prison hides Stand users, devil hosts, and creatures that eat human names. I know you lie awake and listen for footsteps that never stop outside your cell.” The yard noise thins around them. Even the guards lean closer, hungry for Makima’s voice. Jolyne feels the trap inside the kindness. “You talk real sweet for someone who reads people like menus,” she says. Makima steps nearer, and her perfume smells clean, almost kind. “I only want to help you leave this place.” A thin thread slips from Jolyne’s fingertip and tests the air between them. Stone Free hums under her skin, ready to unravel muscle and bone into living string. Makima watches the thread with open fascination. “Beautiful,” she says. “Your body surrenders its shape, yet your will directs every fiber. Most humans only pretend at such control.” Jolyne lets the thread curl around Makima’s wrist without touching skin. “Most humans know the difference between control and ownership.” Makima raises her wrist and studies the string like jewelry. “Ownership is merely control that lasts.” Jolyne snaps the thread back. “Yeah? Put that on a greeting card, bitch.” Makima laughs, quiet and warm, and every nearby inmate smiles without knowing why. “I propose a contract,” she says. “Public Safety clears your name. You see your father. You walk through the front gate before sunset. In return, you obey one order from me, only one, at a time of my choosing.” Jolyne glances at the gate, the sky, the guards, and the too-easy promise. Desire pulls hard in her chest, and Makima watches that pull like a fisherman watches a line. “No details, no limits, no guarantee my dad stays safe?” Jolyne asks. “Trust requires faith,” Makima says. Jolyne grins with all her teeth. “If there’s no Mickey, this shit ain’t Disney!” The smile leaves Makima’s mouth for half a second, and something ancient looks out through her face. Then sweetness returns. “You refuse freedom because the wording displeases you?” “I refuse a leash because you gift-wrap it,” Jolyne says. Makima turns toward Ermes Costello, who waits near the water fountain and pretends not to listen. “Ermes wants the man who kills her sister,” Makima says, still gentle. “One signature gives her his location, his schedule, and a room without cameras.” Ermes goes rigid. Jolyne steps between them. “Don’t,” she warns. Makima keeps her eyes on Ermes. “Loyalty looks heavy, Jolyne. Why carry everyone?” An inmate at the fence begins to cry because Makima promises her dead mother’s voice on a telephone. Another inmate signs Makima’s clipboard for extra food, then immediately offers his bunk, his shoes, and his silence. A guard removes his own cap and holds it like a begging bowl. Jolyne sees the pattern with sick clarity. Makima never raises her voice. She finds the soft, starving place inside each person and puts a finger there. “You don’t help people,” Jolyne says. “You housebreak them.” Makima looks almost pleased. “People relax when someone chooses for them. Choice exhausts dogs and prisoners in equal measure.” Makima lifts one hand, and three inmates step forward in perfect unison. Their eyes shine with devotion, and their feet scrape the concrete together. “Kneel,” Makima tells Jolyne, as politely as a dinner invitation. Pressure fills the air, invisible and total, as if the world agrees that Makima stands above every creature in the yard. Jolyne’s knees tremble. Stone Free bursts from her back in a blue, humanoid rush, and strings pour from Jolyne’s arms, stitching her legs upright and anchoring her to the hoop, the fence, and the ground itself. Jolyne bares her teeth through the strain. “I kneel for nobody.” Makima’s ringed eyes brighten. “Fascinating. You dispute your place.” Jolyne moves first. String whips around Makima’s ankles, then her wrists, then her throat, tightening in a bright web. Guards shout, alarms gather breath, and every inmate freezes. Jolyne pulls, ready to slam Makima face-first into the concrete. Makima does not resist. A thin red line opens at her throat, and at the same instant a prisoner across the yard clutches his neck and falls, choking on blood that belongs to no wound of his own. Makima speaks through the tightening string, calm and clear. “My contract with the Prime Minister converts attacks against me into sickness and accidents among citizens. Harm only travels, Jolyne. It never ends with me.” Horror cools Jolyne’s rage into focus. She loosens the throat string but keeps Makima bound. “You use strangers as armor.” “I use systems,” Makima corrects. She looks at the fallen prisoner with mild regret that imitates compassion perfectly. “It’s okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners.” Jolyne’s stomach turns. “He isn’t yours.” Makima meets her stare. “He asks to be.” Around the yard, inmates nod, guards nod, and even Ermes takes one helpless step toward the clipboard before Jolyne’s string loops her wrist and holds her back. Makima notices, and delight sharpens her sweetness. “You collect strays too. Perhaps you simply resent competition.” Jolyne unravels her left hand completely and sends a hundred threads through the yard. Strings seal mouths before orders escape, bind signing hands, trip advancing feet, and tie every controlled inmate to benches and fences without breaking skin. She moves like a storm with a needle, furious and precise. Makima watches each thread, memorizing range, speed, and weakness. “Your Stand reveals you,” she says. “You unravel before you break. You bind others because abandonment terrifies you.” Jolyne lands close enough to smell Makima’s clean perfume. “And you smile before you bite. Guess we both read.” Makima leans into the web until fresh blood beads along her cheek, and another distant alarm answers from the medical wing. “Release me, or continue and count the cost in strangers,” Makima says. Jolyne holds the tension for one breath, then two, while her friends watch and the controlled inmates strain toward their mistress. Slowly, she withdraws every thread from Makima’s skin and leaves one invisible filament knotted around Makima’s little finger. “Walk away,” Jolyne says. Makima flexes her hand and feels the secret knot sing. Her smile returns, intimate now, almost proud. “You place a leash on me?” Jolyne turns toward her cell block as the fences rattle again around passing prisoners. “No,” she says. “I start a tripwire. Next time you reach for my people, I pull first.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This crossover fic delivers a tense, well-structured confrontation between Jolyne and Makima, staying close to the prompt's specifications: present tense, third person, prison setting, escalating battle of wits, and both characters' canonical abilities (Stone Free's string, Makima's control powers and Prime Minister contract) used accurately and cleverly. Strengths: The prose is clean and controlled, with strong imagery (the "Aquarium" annex, the string-as-tripwire ending). Both voices are distinct and faithful — Jolyne's profanity and defiance ("If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" deployed naturally as a refusal), Makima's soft menace and dehumanizing philosophy. The escalation is logical: offer → refusal → targeting Ermes → mass control → physical confrontation → the contract reveal that harm transfers to innocents → stalemate. The ending is earned and clever: Jolyne leaving a hidden filament on Makima's finger inverts the leash/ownership theme without either character acting out of character. Makima's psychological read of Jolyne ("you unravel before you break... abandonment terrifies you") adds genuine depth. Weaknesses: Some lines lean aphoristic ("Ownership is merely control that lasts") — though this suits Makima, it occasionally tips into neatness. The crowd-control scenes (crying inmate, guard with cap) are efficient but slightly schematic, summarizing rather than dramatized. Minor tell-don't-show moments ("Jolyne feels the trap inside the kindness"). The piece is plot-dense at the expense of atmosphere in the middle. Makima's near-defeat at the end is slightly convenient — she lets Jolyne go a touch easily, though her fascination with a resistant target is canon-consistent. Overall this is a polished, engaging piece with faithful characterization, sharp dialogue, and a satisfying thematic resolution about control versus loyalty. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
SCP-XXXX - Personal Statement of Dr. Elias Vane, Level 3 Researcher, Site-19 Temporal Studies I submitted this account on 14 March, three days after I was removed from active duty and placed under observation in Medical Wing C. I understood why they did it. If I had read this statement from another researcher, I would have recommended the same. The first note appeared on 2 March. I found it folded inside my copy of the Site-19 safety manual, which I kept locked in my desk. I had not opened that drawer in a week, and my office had been searched the previous evening as part of a routine sweep after SCP-████ had attempted to communicate through the ventilation system. > NOTE 1 — Transcribed verbatim: > DO NOT SIGN THE TRANSFER ORDER ON THURSDAY. THE BREACH IS NOT IN CONTAINMENT. IT IS IN THE PAPERWORK. TRUST THE DATE, NOT THE ALARM. > — E.V., 9 March The handwriting was mine. Not similar. Mine. It had the same broken cross on my t's, the same habit of making my capital E look like a reversed 3, even the small ink blot where I always pressed too hard at the start of a signature. I assumed it was a joke, or a test from Internal Security. I logged it, photographed it, and placed it in an evidence sleeve. I told myself I had done the professional thing, and I believed myself until Thursday. On Thursday, Dr. Halvorsen asked me to sign a transfer order moving SCP-████ from Cell 12 to Cell 19 for electrical maintenance. I signed it before I remembered the note. I remembered only when the pen left the page and I saw my signature looked exactly like the blot on the note. Nothing happened. No breach occurred. The transfer proceeded without incident, and I spent that evening wondering whether I had manufactured the memory of the blot to frighten myself. The second note was taped inside my locker on 5 March, although the date at the bottom read 11 March. > NOTE 2: > YOU SIGNED ANYWAY. THAT IS WHY IT HAS TO BE WRITTEN. DO NOT LET THEM MOVE IT BACK ON TUESDAY. IT LEARNED THE ROUTE LAST TIME. > — E.V. I reported it immediately. Security reviewed the locker room footage and found a forty-seven second gap at 03:12. No one entered. No one left. The tape simply jumped, and my locker door, which had been closed, was ajar. That was when the Foundation stopped treating it as a prank. Dr. Halvorsen ordered ink analysis, handwriting comparison, and a full psychological evaluation. The handwriting matched mine with 99.4 percent confidence, including pressure patterns I could not consciously reproduce. The ink analysis was worse. It revealed trace elements not matching any office pen on site: bismuth, vanadium, and a polymer binder discontinued in 1987. My supposed future self was writing with a pen that did not exist in our inventory, and perhaps no longer existed at all. They also considered the alternative. SCP-████ had a documented history of inducing false memories in staff who handled its transfer paperwork. It could not speak, but it had once made a guard believe his daughter had called from inside its cell. The working theory became that the entity was manipulating my perception, planting notes through suggestion, or compelling me to write them during dissociative episodes I did not remember. I was given a cognitive test every morning. I was asked to describe my childhood home, my mother's maiden name, the colour of the Site Director's door. I answered correctly each time. I began to keep my own private log, separate from the official one, because I no longer trusted that I would remember what I had written if someone — or something — altered it. The notes multiplied. I found one in my coat pocket, one under my keyboard, one folded into a paper cup I had just taken from the dispenser. The cup was still warm. > NOTE 5: > HALVORSEN IS DEAD. DO NOT ASK HER ABOUT THE ORDER. IF SHE ANSWERS, LOCK YOURSELF IN THE ARCHIVE AND DO NOT LISTEN TO HER VOICE THROUGH THE DOOR. Dr. Halvorsen was not dead. She brought me coffee twenty minutes after I found that note and asked if I was sleeping. I watched her hands shake slightly from caffeine and tried to decide whether relief or terror was the rational response. If the note lied, then my future self was unreliable. If the note was early, then I was drinking coffee with a woman who would soon die and who might, after that, still answer questions. The Foundation tried to settle it. They moved me to an observation room with continuous recording, no paper, no pens, and a guard who changed every four hours. They gave SCP-████ no contact, no transfers, and no paperwork bearing my name. For two days, nothing arrived. On the third day, I woke with ink on my fingers and a note written on the inside of my own forearm, in handwriting that slanted uphill as if written in a moving vehicle. > NOTE 7 — From forearm, photographed 08:41: > it learns routes it learns names it learns by being moved plese dont let tuesday happen again the breach was march 9 march 11 march march [illegible] i am still in the corridor i can hear me signing That was the last coherent entry they allowed me to transcribe. I still do not know whether I warned myself across time, or whether SCP-████ learned my handwriting the way it learned the transfer route, by being carried through it repeatedly. I only know I stopped trusting the absence of notes more than their presence, because silence began to feel like a page not yet turned. They told me no breach has happened. I believed them. I also kept listening for an alarm that had not sounded, on a Tuesday that, according to every calendar they showed me, had already passed. I still checked every morning twice.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a highly effective SCP-format piece that hits nearly every prompt requirement: escalating notes, contradictory information (Halvorsen dead/alive), Foundation investigation of both temporal anomaly and psychological manipulation by SCP-████, and the researcher's eroding trust in their own perception. The first-person past-tense framing as a "personal statement" submitted after removal from duty is a smart structural choice that gives the account retrospective authority while preserving uncertainty. Strengths: The verbatim notes are genuinely unsettling and escalate well — from clean warnings to the forearm note with deteriorating grammar and illegibility. Specific, concrete details (the 1987-discontinued polymer binder, the 47-second footage gap, the ink blot on signatures) do excellent show-don't-work in establishing authenticity. The Halvorsen note creates a genuinely disturbing paradox ("if the note was early... who might, after that, still answer questions") that lingers. The ending's ambiguity — no resolution, just a researcher checking calendars twice — suits the genre and the prompt's request for perceptual distrust. Weaknesses: The piece is somewhat compressed relative to the 1000-word seed (it's close, actually). The Foundation's investigation is summarized rather than dramatized in places ("They also considered the alternative" is efficient but slightly expository). The middle section's cognitive tests are told more than shown. Some SCP tropes (Site-19, redacted numbers, "routine sweep") are stock, though genre-appropriate. The final line "I still checked every morning twice" is slightly awkward in rhythm. Dialogue is minimal and functional (Halvorsen's coffee moment is the only real exchange), so that criterion is near-irrelevant but what exists is serviceable. Overall this is a polished, controlled piece with strong atmosphere and a satisfyingly unresolved ending appropriate to the format.
